THE DOUBLE LIFE: OR, THE HAMPTON MYSTERY. By the Author of " DAIIKWOOD."

, CHAPTER L. SUCCESS. Joy the lost one is restored! Mits. HEMANS. Lord Grosvenor marked the positions of the re- epective roams of Mrs. Bittly and Wigby by the appearance of the lights, and then stole away cautiously, returning to Bittly, whom he found plunged into the remotest depths of slumber. Satis- fied that hewould not awaken from his drunken trance under several hours, he returned to the house, and waited in the garden until the lights had died out from every room but Giralda's, and until he felt positive that Wigby was asleep. Then he opened and shut the gate, and walked slowly and staggeringly up the path to the front
_ door. He tried the key he had found in Bittly's pocket
after a bungling fashion.

It fitted. He unlocked the door and went into the front hall. It was dark. He slammed the door, being careful not to lock it, and to restore the key to his own pocket, with a view to possibly needing it. He groped along the hall, grumbling in a hoarse voice, as he had heard Bittly grutnole, his hat pulled over his face so as almost to meet his muffler. He had not taken ten blundering steps, when, as he had calculated and hoped, a door was opened at the end of the passage, and Mrs. Bittly betrayed her whereabouts by soundly rating her supposed husband for his delinquencies. -

"The light is out," she exclaimed, wrathfully, "and you needn't think I am going to get up again to light it for you. Keep out of my room, Bittly. I can't a-bear to look at you. There's one comfort —your going to catch what you deserve. Mr. Wigby has written to my lord, and my lord 'II be along afore many hours." Lord Grosvenor grumbled an incoherent re- sponse, and the sound of his incoherent mumbling excited Mrs. Bittly to frenzy. "Oh, you beast !" she ejaculated. "Don't you dare to come into this room. Just you stay there in that hall all night, which I dare say is much better than the place you stayed in last night —you—you yorpus !" Lord Grosvenor obeyed her energetically de- livered command, sinking heavily and like a dog on the cold hall-floor, and soon after producing an excellent imitation of Bittly's heavy breathing, as at that moment practised under the neighbouring hedge. "There be goes." cried the irate Mrs. Bittly— "a tuning of his pipes! Well, he's safe for to- night; but won't he catch it in the morning, both from my lord and me?" She turned over in the bed, her last reflection being to her disturbed soul like oil poured upon the waters, and after a long period of tossings and mutterings, she dropped in to heavy sleep. Then Lord Grosvenor, who had been as watch- ful and wakeful as a lynx. raised himself slowly on his elbow, waited a little while, and then cautiously and softly arose to his feet. "She is asleep," he thought," I must have that key from her dress pocket. It is time to move." He stole into the bedroom silently. A dim light struggled through the curtained window. He could see plainly the shrouded bed in the corner, with its heavily slumbering occupant. He could also see the chair upon which she had cast off her garments. Her gown lay on the top, plainly in view. Ile crept towards it. He searched its folds for the pocket, found it, and withdrew the key. Then he stole again to the door, and paused on

the threshold. His light movements had not disturbed the woman. Her breathing was louder and more regular than before. "I'll make sure that she does not interrupt me," he thought, feeling for the key in the lock. "I do not mean to run any unnecessary risks." He deftfy transferred the key to the outer side of the lock, passed into the hall drew the door and locked it.

Then he paused to listen again. The woman had not been in the slightest degree disturbed by his operations. Breathing a sight of thankfulness, he stole up stairs to the door of that upper chamber, the win- dow of which he had seen boarded over, and tapped softly. Then there was a sound as someone astir within. Then he inserted the key cautiously in the lock, turned the bolt and opened the door gently, repeat- ing his low knock. Having opened the door, he paused on the thres- hold, calling. in a whisper:

" Giralda-1"- There came a low cry from within the chamber, a quick spring, and Giralda—palg, agitated, and strangely lovely in a sudden bright expectancy— pulled the door open wider and confronted him. For one brief instant she stood in wild amaze- ment, staring at the uncouthly disguised figure, hd sold in her eyes, and then Lord Grosvenor tore the muffler from his face, the hat from his head, and stood before her, brave, eager, noble, and impassioned, with radiant eyes and smiling lips. How the oollour hindered up into the girl'spure cheeks, like a red light flickering through an ala- baster shade ! How her eyes glowed! How her pure and lovely face beamed! Lord Grosvenor held out his arms. She sprang Into there, and nestled close to his broad young breast. "Oh, Paul I knew you would come !" she murmured in a happy contentment. "I knew that you were looking for me, and that you would find me I" Her joy overflowed in happy tears. "You are safe now, my darling !" said Lord Grosvenor, his joy as great as her own, and equally apparent. "Thank Heaven I have found you You cannot know what I have suffered since I learned of your disappearance from the Park. But the light has come at last!" He gathered her into a passionate embrace, and showered kisses on her dusky head, on her brows, on her face, all the while breathing tender epi- thets and loving assurances. At last he released her, remembering that they were not yet safe. "Where is Fay ?" he asked. Giralda led him to the bedside. Fay was lying on the couch, fully dre.,sed, his violet eyes closed In sleep, his golden hair drifting over his pillow. " Waken him, darling !" said Grosvenor softly. Giralda bent over the little fellow, rousing him gently. She hushed the outcry he would have made instinctively on beholding a stranger at his bedside at that hour, and with tears and smiles and blushes told him that their deliverer had come —that Lord Grosvenor was here. Fay was awake immediately. "Let me carry him down," suggested the young lord. "There will be fewer steps to arouse Mrs. Bittly and Wigby." Fay assented, and Grosvenor took him up in his arms. "Are you all ready, Giralda?" asked her lover. _ _ _

"All ready, Paul, excepting my hat and cloak," answered Giralda, proceeding to don those. "I had not undressed. I was sleepless, and so sat up to read." She was soon ready. Then Grosvenor, extinguish- ing the light, led the way down stairs, Giralda following like a shadow. They b tole along the hall, out of doors, down the garden walk, and into the road; and now the maiden began to breathe more freely. She looked up at the sky, with the gray clouds flitting over Ii; back at the square brick house where she had endured her painful captivity ; and then she clung to the young lord's arm in a trans- port of delight. "0, Paul ! " she murmured, "now indeed I feel that I am safe." "And so do 1," put in Fay's small voice, from Grosvenor's bosom. "And, if you please, Paul, I'll get down and do my own walking. lam too old and too heavy to be carried like a chili." Grosvenor laughed, and put the boy down, keep- ing fa., t hold of his tiny hand, and the three walked en together. "I thought it strange when you knocked so softly at my door, Paul," said Giralda, leaning on his arm. "Mrs. Bittly never knocked at all. "I borrowed it of Bittly himself. He is waiting for it under this hedge,". responded our hero, smil- ing. "Wait here a moment while I exchange with Giralda." Christmas has come and gone, but not the Christmas dances and parties, and no doubt most of us are looking forward to some of these delight- fel events. And the first question that arises is, of course What shall we go in? I must tell you of a dress-frock suitable for a Cinderella dance. It is very simple and pretty, and really quite easy to make. There are some very pretty tinsel gauzes sold at quite a low price, and if they are made over a cheap silk foundation, or even a good and bright sateen, they look as nice as if they had cost very much more. I will suppose that this dress is made of these materials, the foundation in a rather deep pink shade, the overskirt having silver and pink tinsel stripes on a white groundwork. Round the bottom of the skirt is arranged a pleat- ing of pink satin ribbon, on which are sewn tiny pink rosebuds and a few green leaves. A full sash of soft pink silk is tied round the waist, and finished off at the ends with a fringe of glittering silver bangles. The bodice is simply gathered bebe fashion, and a double frill, arrranged to form sleeves and bertne, has a narrow heading of pink roses. . _ _

Another evening costume—and this is suitable for nearly every evening occasion—has a plain soft green satin skirt, velvet waistband, and a love of a bodice, draped with pure white and pink em. broidered lisse—what is known as broderie Anglaise.

While alluding to evening attire, I cannot do better than describe an evening cloak I was awfully taken with last week. It was made of white nun's veiling, lined with pink silk. The yoke was of white and pink brocade, and the cape edged all round with white Thibet. This cape can be suc- cessfully copied in brown cloth, lined pink and trimmed mink, or in velveteen, trimmed blue fox, or black Thibeb, according to the shade chosen. It could, I should think, be easily made at home, and if fashioned in velveteen, would be suitable for wearing at any time.

A charming evening frock for a debutante is made of rich white satin duchess°. The sleeves are, of course, full, and the neck out not too low. It is prettily trimmed with strings of pearls and Fedora lace.

It is an ..aom, think, that you cannot possibly look well attired unless your hair is properly dressed. The most fashionable kind of headdress Ii either n single or double bandeau, sometimes draped with gauze, with a large butterfly or aigrette at the aide, or a spray of flowers. Un- married girls, as a rule do not wear jewels. But there are a. variety of fascinating aigrettes of various kinds and colours, which are becoming. Bows of pearls or small fine chains, intereplrsed With pearls end turquoise, are usually worn round the neck.

-- ----- Th. very prettiest hat I have seen this season had • brim of gathered black velvet, a crown of rose pink velvet, and black feathers and satin rib- bons. The way in which the brim was curved was quite perfect, with a little dip over the right eye, a deeper one over the right ear, end • dainty fold of pink velvet lifting the whole at the left side. The lovely soft, dark hair beneath was arranged with the usual (artificial) crinkles, and was drawn back into the ohignon in those harmonious. lines that are half the charm of a skilfully-arranged coiffure. Do you know what I mean? Sometimes the hair is dragged up in one place, straight back In another, and drawn down behind the ears. When it is all combed back in one direction, the lines all running one way, the effect is a hundred

The following treatment is said to be effective :—Cut a hole in a piece of leather sufficiently large enough to pass the wart through, then mix the following on a piece of glass—a small quantity of flour of sulphur, with equal parts of water and sulphuric acid to a thick paste. Then place the leather over the wart and apply the ointment with a stick ; be careful not to get it on your Angers. After the application remove the leather. In ten or twelve: minutes apply a little lard or sweet oil. One application usually is sufficient to remove any ordin- ary wart. Great care must be taken in handling the acid.
A New Game.

The first game is called the '-'-Alphabet "—not a bad name to begin our list with—and our seven or eight players can draw round the fire and warm their toes, I while the first player calls out some letter if the alphabet the next player adds to this another letter, which,added to that one, will form part of some word he thinks of. The third player then adds a letter under the same con- ditions ; and so on. In course of time someone has to add the letter that completes a word, and this last man is out of the game; only, of course, as far as hi s turn goes; the winner being the last left in, and he starts the next word. For instance, the first player may start off with a C, the second venture on H, the third I, the fourth M, the fifth N, the sixth E, the seventh is obliged to finish up with a Y, unless he can think of any other letter making a longer word, this being the first letter that forms the whole into a word, he is out of the game. If the fourth player had said N instead of M, he would have spelt Chin; he would have been out and the fifth player have started another word. As I said at starting, this game requires just a little thought, especially after the first two or three letters.—Little Folks.

Symptoms of Fever. Sometimes the. occurrence of a "rigor," or shivering fit, is the first decided indication the patient has of something being svionF.f. The onset of this condition is, says "The Family Physician," not infrequently . abrupt and striking, the patient passing in to it at ' once from the slight and scarcely appreciable dis- order of the preliminary stage, or even from a state ! of seeming health. Sometimes, on the contrary, the chill is so slight, and is so intiniately associated with the premonitory symptoms of which we have spoken, that it is irnpoSsible to decide on the exact time of its , occurrence. In some cases there is simply a greater sensitiveness of the surface to the impression of cold, so that a current of cool air or the contact of a cold body produces a feeling of chilliness which runs momentarily tnrough the frame, and then subsides. The sense of cold, however, is usually more permanent, and quite independent of surrounding objects. It begins most commonly in the back, and extends to the limbs and over the body, producing chattering of the teeth, and sometimes universal tremor and sahking ; and this may occur although the patient may be near the fire or covered with blankets in bed. In some fevers the rigors are more intense, and of far more constant occur- rence than in others. In smallpox they are definite :TM prolonged, and in typhus they' are frequently well marked. In scarlet fever, diphtheria, measles, and acute dysentery, there may be a distinct rigor or only a passing sensation of chilliness. Typhoid fever usually commences insidiously, but in the cases in which the onset is sudden a shivering fit is not of infrequent occurrence. The cold stage of ague may he said to he composed of a succession of rigors. It is not im pro- probable that shivering fits are induced more readily in some constitutions than in others. The mere snipping of a blister—an operation which it is needless to say is perfectly painless—will in many people so far throw the nervous system off its balance as to produce a rigor. Some individuals are so delicately organised that they can never pass water in the open air without experiencing a transitory feeling of chilliness.

div.head: OUR BOYS AND GIRLS.
div.p: OUR BOYS AND GIRLS.

When a son, grown to manhood, leaves the paienta r-of to take up life's fight for himself, both mother and father keenly feel the loss. Perhaps the father carries himqelf in a matter-of-course way, slaps the young fellow on the shoulder and wishes him luck, but the mother sheds many a tear all to herself. She bore him, nursed him, pulled him through his illness, and lugged him about on her tireless left arm. He is her " baby " still, and as he goes he takes a big piece of her heart with him.

But she mourns the girls even more, when they aban- don her. That is why a wedding in the old home, a daughter being the bride, is proverbially as sad as a funeral. Yet, in one way or another, the young people go, God help us! and leave father and mother alone with their grey hairs and their memories. A father who came near losing a beloved daughter with disease speaks of it thus : " Oar Anna," he says, " had an attack of influenza in October, 1889. Her f ->od did not nourish her, and in spite of all we eould do she wasted away until she was thin and wan and weak. Her hands and feet were cold and clammy—she was always cold, notwithstanding extra flannels and clothing. A little later she became so emaciated that it did not seem as though she had any life left in her. She lost all her bright spirits and was listless and help- ' less. At this time she was about sixteen years of age.

" Then her breathing got hard and difficult, and it was painful to hear her. Neat her legs became swollen and puffe(l, and she could only walk a few yards. Abscesses began to form on her legs, arms, neck, and ankles. They finally CAME) tO be about as large as eggs—about three inches in diameter. Nearly a pint of matter came away from some of them. At length the poor child bad twenty-four of these on her body. "For weeks and weeks she lay on the couch, sinking l gradually until she looked like death. Wife and I felt like having to give her up. During eighteen months it took my wife an hour, night and morning, to dress these terrible and painful abscesses. At first we had a doctor from Faringdon, but she got no better from his treatment. He recommended us to get her into a hosp..:, tal, but we did nest like to let her go. We next tried a doctor at Stanford, He attended her twelve months, but she got worse and worse. What more to do we did not know. It seemed as though she was surely doomed to die. Yet help came when we had stopped looking for it. " In December, 1891, we heard of Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, and the great things it had done after medical men had failed. We got the medicine from Messrs. Ballard and Ca., Chemists, Paringdon, :and she commenced taking it. In a few weeks we noticed a great improvement in her general health. He food digested and strengthened her and in two months we could see the abscesses dying away, and soon they were all gone. "She is now as strong as ever site was, and is the picture of heatlh. My wife and I, also everyone in the village, look upon the cure as miraculous. That Mother Seigel saved Anna's life we are fully persuaded. You are at liberty to publish this statement. I will gladly answer any inquiries. Yours truly tsigued), Isaac King, innkeeper, Horn Inn, Charney, Berks, November 25th, 1892." Mr. King is happy over this splendid result. Who would not be, in his place 2 But there was no miracle. What the Syrup did was on Nature's straight lines. His dauehter's case was one of blood poisoning from the deadly acids engendered by the non-digestion of her fond Probably it had been coming on, unsuspected, longer than her parents thought. The danger to her life was great ; indeed, death was certain in a little more time. Most fortunately they heard of Seigel'a Syrup before it was quite too late. This magnificent remedy expelled the poison from the blood, and by righting the digestion prevented the for- !nation of more. Long may the family circle continue unbroken.

ments, and took back his own. "Where are we going now, Giralda ?" asked Fey, gravely. "I don't know,' returned Giralcia, conten- tedly. "It's all right though, Fay. Paul knows." Her trust in her lover gave her a delicious sense of restfulness, very refreshing after her late deso- lation and confinement. That had been a dark day with her. Mrs. Bittly had been insolent and harsh, and had more than once, to show off her authority, declared she should shut Fay up in an entirely separate apartment—a threat which had agonized Giralda, and almost broken the little lads' heart. And DOW- she could hardly realize it— they were free, safe, and together. "Paul is all well enough, remarked Fay, after a thoughtful pause, his violet eyes shining with a wistful light. "He's good, Giralda ; and I love him ; but," and the little voice quivered, "I want mamma." Grosvenor returned in time to hear this piteous lament. "Just keep up your courage, Fay, a little longer," he said cheerfully, "and you shall see her. I promised her that I would bring you to her at ten o'clock this morning." Fay's sobs gave way to a gleeful cry. • "You promised mamma that ?" asked Girsida, as they walked on. "When did you see her, Paul ?' "To-day—this afternoon." Giraida thrilled with a joyful excitement. "Where is she ?" she questionee. "At Hamptonwold, only a few miles from here. Lord Hampton and Lord Trevelyan are also there."

Giralda began to tremble. "I cannot meet Uncle Trevelyan l" she exclaimed. "Paul, what does all this mean ?" "It means, darling, that the Lady Beatrice will see you secretly in her garden. She has been almost crazed about you and Fay. She received your letter, that you were in Dalton with Fay safe. I told her yesterday that you were missing again. Having company, she cannot get away to see you. I must take you both to her." "Will this secrecy ever end ?" cried Giralda, passionately. "Oh, if papa could only stand among men stainless in name. Why must that guilty man always triumph?" "His hour is approaching Giralda," said her lover. "He is drawing near to the end. His very desperation of late proves it." He told her then how he had sought for her ; how he had received her letter; and how he had traced her to her prison. "And papa, and Rupert? They are safe in the country 1' "They are at the Eagle's Eyrie. They will be at Hamptonwold this morning, it is after mid- night now. The Lady Beatrice wants to assemble her little family together once more in secret before they are again separated." "Poor mamma 1 What is going to become of us all?" "Mr. Trevelyan will take his children abroad, you with the others, Qiralda. And I shall go, too, and, if you will, your parents have consented that in some pleasant foreign town you and I shall be married. You will be safe from Adlowe's perse- cutions only as my wife. Are you willing, dar- ling? Will you soon give me that priceless treas- ure—yourself ?" He bent low over her, looking one of those bebouair knights of long ago, his noble face aglow, his dusky eyes full of loving light. It was not to be wondered at that Giralda hung her head shyly, and blushed, and gave an assent so timid that only ears rendered keen by love could have told the whisper from a sigh. We will not attempt to depict the lover's rap- ture, nor his expression of it. They walked along as if treading on air, forget- ful of all save each other, when the lagging steps of Fay recalled the young lord to the fact that the child was growing tired. Disregarding the little fellow's grave remon- strances, Grosvenor took him up again, and the boy dropped asleep on his shoulder. "Where are you taking us now ? " asked Giralda. "To the inn." "It must be closed at this hour," said the young girl, with a sense of embarrassment growing upon her. "0, Paul what will they say to our arrival at this hour, and on foot ? " "I will make it all right, Giralda," responded her young lover. "We have really no other place to go, and we cannot spend the night out of doors. Leave it all to me." By this time they were nearing the outskirts of Pencoed. They had met no one on the way, but now the clatter of hoofs on the road attracted their attention. "Someone is about to meet us," said Lord Gros- venor. " Adlowe has been sent for. It may be he. It is certainly not an hour for people to be out on ordinary pursuits. He looked about him. There was a gap in the Ledge at one side of the road. He drew Giralda through the aperture, and they both crouched in the shadow of the hedge and watched the road. The horseman, whose coming they had heard, came slowly round a curve in the road, and rode past them, directing his course toward Giralda's late prison. The steed he bestrode was faded and wet with foam. He had evidently come a considerable journey. The face of the man was turned slightly toward them. It was the face of Lord Adlowe. They waited until he had passed out of sight, and then emerged from their concealment. Giralda was pale, but courageous. "We must hasten to the inn," said Grosvenor, quickly. Once there, he cannot touch you. Come.l', They hurried over the road, entered the town, and reached the inn. The landlord was in the act of closing his door. He was already aware of the feet that his guest was noble, and a friend of the Hamptons. His inn was leased from the Lady Beatrice, it being her own private property. Her ladyship's name was, therefore, an "open sesame" to his house and heart. "This young lady and gentleman, landlord," said Lord Grosvenor, are on their way to Hamp- tonwold, by invitation of the Lady Beatrice Hampton. They have met with a misfortune by which they were obliged to complete their journey on foot. They require adjoining rooms—your beat —and in the morning, about eight o'clock, a car- riage and driver." Giralda'a appearance was sufficient to proclaim her a lady. The landlord did not pause to reflect upon the singularity of hr late arrival on foot, accepting Grosvenor's statement without question. Indeed, Lord Grosvenor, young as he was, was not a man whose word could be doubted. A maid was summoned, rooms were got ready, and in half an hour Giralda and Fay were both

asleep. Unknown to them, or to any one, Lord Gros- venor, apprehensive of Adlowe's pursuit, posted himself in the hall, outside Giralda's door, and watched and waited—a sleepless, tireless sentinel. (To be continued).

In London and other large towns of England, Scot- land, and Wales, military drill is, says "Chums,' now compulsory for telegraph messengers. There are no fewer than 3,500 of these lads between four teen and eighteen years of age in London alone, who are discip- lined and trained in exercises exactly similar to those which young soldiers have to undergo. They are drilled in squads, companies, and battalions; they have district parades from time to time, and on such occasions they have been complimented by their inspecting officers. A representative of "Chums" was favoured by Lieut-Col. J. P. MacGregor, of the Post Office Volunteers, with an interview on the subject. " Tte drilling of telegraph messengers." said Colonel MacGregor, "is not a wholly new arrangement, though the present system only came into operation about two years ago. When the tele' graphs were taken over by the State, it was noticed that the boys who had been in the employ of the old companies were rather slovenly looking and, in order to smarten them, drills were instituted. These, however, were discontinued after two or three years. When Sir James Fergusson was Postmaster-General, he, as an eld army officer—he was wounded at Inkerman—thought there was room for improvment in the appearance of the boys, and:the present system of drills is the result of the interest he took in the subject. His idea was that drill would not only improve the physique of the boys but brighten them up in other respects ; and Mr. VVal- pole, the present Secretary of the G.P.0., also gives his personal encouragement to the scheme. The details were, for the most part, left to myself to work out ; and one of the changes introduced as regards the uniform of the messsengers was the replacement of the shoulder- strap by a belt with a buckle. The brightness of the buckle and the metal buttons which are now worn on the uniform is a good test of the tidiness of the boys. Arrangements have been made whereby, in London, the boys are drilled in places as near where they live as possible. These inelude Chelsea, Wellington, Kensing- ton, and St. John's Wood Barracks, the Tower, and the Volunteer drill-halls. The messengers can be drilled at the rate of 1,000 per week, so that each boy is exercised in company drill once or twice every third week. The companies have a total of fifty-six each -- fifty in the ranks, two subalterns, two guides, and tvio markers. In addition every boy as he comes on duty daily, is inspected, to see if his uniform and equipment are in Prder. If possible, he is also put through a few minutes' drill. Each district has its own drum and fife hand. In some cases the messengers themselves con- tribute a fund for the payment of the instructors, in others the instruction is given free. Both physical drill and the manual exercise are taught with Martini-Henry , carbines, 1,000 of which have been lent by the War I Office. To prevent the possibility of danger, should there be any disposition to play pranks with the carbines eare has been taken to make firing them as in possibility. The carbines are similar to those used in cadet corps. There is this difference between the telegraph messengers and ordinary cadets as regards drill, that in the latter case it is voluntary, in the former it is compulsory. Possibly it is because of this that a very mistaken idea widely prevails. Many people suppose, because the telegraph boys must drill, that they will have to join the army. There is no such regulation. There was, for a time, a schedule under which, when boys reached the age of sixteen, they were told that while only a propor- tion of their number could be retained in the service of

the Post Office when they attained the age-limit of eigh- teen, yet, if they chose to join the army, employment would be found for them when their service with the colours expired. That schedule has been rescinded,and no boy is asked or counselled to join the army. The drills have been ins'zituted solely for the benefit of the boys themselves, to improve their physique, to smarten them, and to make them take a proper pride in them- selves. As inducements prizes are offered, and amongil those given have been bound volumes of "Chums.' 'That the boys have benefited by the training they are now receiving is evident from their appearance and bearing. Certainly they are much superior in this respect to other boys of their own class.

Bd. per week, he felt that the committee weredoing right as Mr. Bamber was an excellent officer, and had shown marked.ability. He had had his salary raised from E 53. to 30s. in 1891. He might mention that St. George's Mission new school had been opened far children during the present week. • CouncillorSztmcocx seconded, and the minutes were ' passed. MUSEUM &C.., COMMITTEE AND CEMETERY coimarrEs. The minutes of these committees, which appeared in our last issue., were passed, the former on the motion , of Councillor ROBERTS seconded by Councillor GREENING, and the latter on the motion of Alderman HARRISON seconded bq Councillor BILL TOWN HALL, &C., COMMITTEE. Alderman Bovromin moving the adoption of this Com- mittee's 'minutes, said that he considered that the pro- posed alterations to the baths were reasonable. As to the resolution of the Council with reference to the conversion of the stables at the Town Hal into munici- pal ofices,the Committee had taken it into consideration thoroughly, and they were unanimous that they were not suitable for the purpose. With regard to the pro- posal to increase the bands' subscription from £2O to £5O per aunum,s, deputation 'from the bands' association had waited upon the Committee saying that £2O was insuffi- cient ;and they had to go tround with the hat to raise sufficient funds. . .

CounCiiiOr CANNELL -seconded the passing of the minutes. The MAZIlit explained that the bands would not only plarinthe park, hut in the open spaces of the town as well, and bethought that4£so was not too much to give them. Councillor 'Losorox Wished to know why the stables at the Town Nall were mit suitable for conversion into Offices. . . . .

Councillora. T. FitieCLOurie said that he had received a small Sketch from Mr. Woods, member of the Royal &cademy with respect LA the extension of the Town Hall. Be would be pleased to show it to any member of the ,Council. This gentleman was the highest authority as to the ,character the ewtension should be and it wotild be worth,while to study it. 'CouncllioraonEervalso thought that the Committee •shodl&haye stated why they considered the proposal was not suitable. Reestill thought that they were mak- ing Iv great anistakcjin. nOt alto ng plans to be submitted to the• Council for consideration with respect to ,munici- pal,ciffices. .He thought that it would be a wise thing if the Council passed plans before any further great ex- penditure of money was made to show to the people that something worthy of the town would PIN) ,carried out. . . . . .
Coundillor Bataturrr thought that the site .df the

stables was very convenient. alderman BotareN in reply said that the stables were •unsuitable because they were too far away, and as they tbad other more convenient buildings a short distance away, they considered that they would be better for the ,purpose of municipal offices. MARKETS COMMITTEE.—PROPOSES') cArrLE MARKET.

Alderman.Boseartuesr proposed the adoption of the .minutes which appeared in our last issue. Iffe•remarked 'that the Committee had had to consider the provisions of a suitable site tor a cattle market, and they had ac- cordingly loosed all round the borough and inspected -several, places with this view. They had found that the Militia Barracks was the best site, inasnauch are itwas near the railway station and had god approaches' from all parts of flee town. The committee considered that it was the beat site they could possibly have selected, and the cost was less than any other place that could have been got. It was about 7,000 or B,OtN) square yards in extent, and would cost £5,700. This sum sinCluded the price of the site, also £BOO for paving the yard and sheds, and£lso for fitting up the necessary-stalls, eke. 'Upon the site were eostly buildines, which had cost be- tween£7;ooo and £B,OOO to erect, and these codlcteasily be converted into a cattle market. He thoueht if the Council adopted the recommendations of the Committee they would be able to convert the barracks into such a market that it would be second to none in lLoneashire. The market would have to be ereeted within the borough to enable the Corporotion to levy tolls. It was not desired to make a profit out of the tolls. The only object was to regulate trade and to meet the requirements of the Board of Trade. :X had been suggested that the market should be on the Cheshire side of the borough, but it had apparently been overlooked that animals sold would have to be brought over the bridge and into the town. Then with regard to the cost of the barracks, whick,he had already stated, vould be about £5,700, assuming that thirty years were allowed for the repayment of themoney, thov would have to pay in the way of sinking fund and interest E 290 per annum, or in round numbers .2300. To meet this there would be the rentstfrom the cottages situated in the barracks, which last year realized £ll6 10a. 10d ; rent of the technical instruction school, £5O ; and the tolls from the sales of cattle would be at ',east £lOO. If a cattle market was not provided the Corporation would have to put down weighing machines at the Pig Market, at the cattle fair, and in two places where the sales were held. Councillor FIEPHERD seconded. Councillor Dr. CANNELL moved an amendment zo the effect that the minutes of the Markets Committee be confirmed with the exception of the resolution of•the 'l7th .December having reference to the report of the sub-committee on the provision of a cattle market. 'He contended that as the Council bad rejected a similar motion•some time ago,they had no right to pass it now. The houses inside the barracks were not habitable, and it was R ell.known that they hadone of the worst sewers In Wilsen-Patten-st., being at the present moment little better than a cesspool. He was of opinion that the barracks would be inadequate for the purposes of a cattle market. Couneillorligaeore seconded the amendment and re- marked that he had never seen a cattle market walled in by a ten or eleven-foot wall. If they made the tar- reeks into a market, such a wall would surrolandit, and would nrevent plenty fresh air from getting to the animals. Fle thought that a sufficiently large number of animals was not brought to Warringtoa to cover the cost of the ventiire, and that the Council would rue the -day if they decided mat the barracks were suitable tor a market. If such a market Was placed there, it would have thecffect of depreciating the property in the neigh- bourhood by some £3,000 or £4 000. It would also be extremely unhealthy for the school children at the People's College and Trinity Schools. Alderman Yemmoite was fully convinced that the Corporation ought to buy the Barracks, hut not for the purposes of a cattle market. They heard a great deal about the Bridewell, and he thought the Barracks might be bought for the purposes of the police. With regard to the purchase of the Barracks, he had reason to believe that the property had been actually purchased, and he thought it was a wrong principle for two or three people to pledge the Council to any- thing. The Marne I have -purchased the nreperty myself, and if the Corporation will not take it, I will take it myself. (Hear, hear.) Alderman FRANCOIrn hoped the Council would In the right thing, but he did .not think the barracks were suitable For a cattle market, Councillor SKELTON theueit the members of the Coun- cil ought to protest againet the expenditure of the large: amount of money proposed unless they were thoroughly satisfied that the cattle market would be self-supporting. He contended that the scheme would not be self-sup- portino. He then proceeded to refer to the probable sources of income from different sources, the, figures he gave making a gross income of £2lO. The cost of the building would be quite £7,000. Then there would be the maintenance charges. They would want one or two men to look after the place, and that would cost at least £lOO per annum. De Corporation would also loose be abolishing the sales at the Norton Arms Hotel and the Eagle and Child Inn by £7O, because they were entitled to collect that amount without providing a place. The cost of the Corporation would be OM per annum, a net loss of £l7O, and against, that they would not get '5O cattle per week to sell, for the reason that the various auctioneers would make other arrangements by taking their sales to Stockton Heath or Stretton. Councillor Sturm:rosy supported the amendment, say- na that the Corporation had bought quite enough land in the borough to supply all requirements. Councillor PLIMPTON thought the purchase of the barracks was a very good one indeed. The land alone would have been cheap at the price, even if there were no buildings upon it. A better spot, in fact, rould not have been found. With regard to the sewers, they were not I,kely to have such high tides as previously, as the Shin Canal had done away with that. They must find a fresh place for their pig market. as it was a nuisance to Town Bill, as also Was the fair in Winwick-street. He did not think that a better place could be found than the barracks. Councillor LONGTON ask,rl the Chairman if he Was willine to nut the rnaohition in such a form as Would

enable them to buy the place without being prejudiced In his opinion, the purchase was not at all a dear one,but the property might be utilized for other porn a than those of a cattle market. He shoild certainly alipoort the purchase, if the question a: to how the propvrty should be utilized was postpened. Alderman flurcuttiscia observed that he had beea a member of the Markets Committee for twelve years,and was sorry that on this occasion he had to oppose the members. Before the barracks cluld be cotnpl,tely cln- verted into a cattle market, 28.000 would bespe'tt. He thought they had not had sufficient information on the matter, and that it ought to have been previously discussed. _ • . .

Councillor Beam Err asked is he would be in order if he moved another amendment, that the barracks be purchased, but that the expediency of using it for the purpose of a cattle market be deferred. Alderman BrAcencasr replied that before it was so used the question would be submitted to the Council. Councillor WOODS spoke in support of the minutes, and contended that so far from being a loss, the cattle ' market would be a source of profit. He was delighted to hear that they had such a public-spirited Mayor as Councillor Fairclough to puchase property, and retain It for the benefit of the town. Councillor ROBERTS said he thought that all the mem- bers of the Council believed that the purchase as a per- chase was a desirable one, and ought not to be missed. kt the same time he W4B not prepared that night to sup- port absolutely, its use for the purpose indicated. He thought the question should be left over. Alderman BLACICHIIRST promised that the storehouse should not he used as a cattle market until the matter had again been brought under the notice of the Council. Councillor Roasars said that that relieved him from a diffieulty,and after the distinct statement of the Chair- man of the committee tie should support the confirmation of the minutes. Alluding to the buying of the property by the Corporation, Councillor Roberts said that when it became known that the Corporation as a Corporation wanted to purchase property, something like 60 per cent, was put upon the value at once. It was, therefore, desirable that these matters should be arranged quietly. They were indehted to the Mayor for his action in the present matter, and personally he was obliged to him. He hoped they would net let the purchase slip. He re- ferred to the necessity which existed for some portion of the premises being used for a technical school. They were in the building on sufferance at the present time, and could be turned out at a moment's notice. The Committee were, therefore, willing to meet the Markets Committee in the matter. With regard to Alderman Mitchinson's remarks concerning the school children who attended Poople's College and Trinity schools, he said he had carried on business at the end of Wilson Patten-st.. Tor a considerable number of years, and lie could assure the Council that the majority of children from the two important schools that had been named did not go down the street. Alderman BOLTON who was received with cries of Vote, vote," said that they would have to wait till he hadfinished. He contended that the committee should withdraw the suggested use of the building as a cattle market. Let the matter be left in the hands of the ,General 'Purposes Committee for the purchase of the 'property at some time or other. Alderman BLACRHURST remarked that Councillor Skelton was alt ',gecher at sea with regard to the 'figures he ha used ; bet he promised that before the building was used as a cattle market, the matter should againte brought under the notice of the Council. He would add to his original motion the words :—" Upon the condition that before the storehouse is used as a cattle 'market the application of the premises shall he submitted again to the Council." This was seconded by Councillor HEPHERD. Alderman BLACKHURST said Councillor Skelton had stated that the number of cattle sold was not 50 per week. They however had it on undoubted authority that it was 657 a week. The tells would be £3 14s. 4d. per week. The motions were then put to the meeting. The amendment of Dr. Cannell was submitted first, and the voting resulted as follows :—For : Aldermen Francotnb,Bolton and Hutchinson; Councillors Carmen, Hill, Smethurst, Shillcock, Bennett, Shaw, Skelton, Baird, Wilkinson, and Heaton-13. Against : Aldermen Harrison, Blackhurst and Sutton ; Councillors Fair- dough, Roberts, Greening Plumpton, Shaw Green, Longton, Lee, Evans, Woods, Beaman, Hepherd, and the Mayor-15. The amendment was therefore lost. Alderman Blackhurst's motion, with the addition 'named, was then put and carried.

div.head: EVE.
div.p: EVE.

Alderman HUTCHINSON moved, and Councillor SMET- IIIIEST seconded the passing of the minutes, which were of aroutine character. Councillor GREENING asked the Chairman of the Com- mittee how it was that the fire brigade were so long before they were able to play upon the recent fire in 'Johnson's yard ? Messrs. Johnson had lost a large lump of money. He would not say through the negligence of -the men, but through the delay which arose, and the committee had spent a large sum of money on the pur- chase of a new engine lately. Councillor nominees asked whether there were any means of attaching sxne kind of bags to the fire engine to prevent the wheels getting on fire, and if there were, how was it that they were not attached on the night of the fire? 'Councillor WOODS: Is it true that after a man has rune the bell to give the alarm of fire he has to bolt to the fire engine station to sign a document before the fire en gine is turned out ? If that is so it is very peculiar. A place may be burned down in the meantime. Is it also a fact that the men were going about all night try- ing to purchase coal in Rose and Crown-se., and Bank. St. and other equally eminent places ? (Laughter.) Alderman Hurcunisme said he could reply to each ,question from his knowledge of the circumstances of the case. Immediately the firebell was rung on New Year's Eve the horses weee in readiness and were harnessed and attached to the fire engine even before it was known where the fire was. Consequently, there was no neglect onthe part of the superintendent of the fire brigade that the brigade were not at the scene of the fire earlier. They were there within a few minutes after the ringing of the fire-bell. Councillor Plumpton had asked a question with reference to the bags. They were not at the fire just in time, but they were there afterwards. With regard to the question which Councillor Woods had asked he might say that'it was not necessary te sign a paper before the fire engine was used in Warrington ; it was necessary to do so in the case of fires which occurred out of the borough. That had been an old rule which was found necessary to adopt to get the expenses from those hung out of the town for the use of the engine. With reference tc the remarks which have been made about the abort supply of coal, he was at the fire about a quar- ter to ten. The engine was then working well, and there was plenty of coal, but afterwards when the engineer said that they were short of coal he (Alderman Hutchinson) went tl a neighbouring public-house and asked for some coal so that the firemen might not be taken awav from their work. The motion for the confirmation of the minutes was then put and carried. WATER COMMITTEE. Alderman 7RANCoMe moved the confirmation of the Water Committee's minutes. He said he believed that the ten per cent, would pay very well, and also relieve the committee of a great deal of trouble. The committee were anxious to get the lock-up shops to take a supply. The charge was half the domestic rate on the assessment. They were anxious that the whole town should have a good supply of water, and they hoped that some of the leading shop keepers would help them in the matter, and do their utmost to set a good example. Let them never mind the little extra cost to themselves. The committee were paying a large sum—£4,s79 lla. 61.—in interest on the annuities, hut he was glad to say that the income from the Water Works was very much more than enough to pay every charge. The committee had reasou to believe that they had a very successful undertaking, and that when they were called upon to pay for the sinking fund that they would be able to do so without putting any extra charge on the rates of the town. Coe nci I lor HEPREnn seconded. Councillor SHAW asked what the exact profit was for the last twelve months. Alderman FRA.NCOMB: Mr. Shaw can get the informa- tion from the Borough Treasurer. If he will put the qu,stion as a motion we will give him the exact figures of profit made on the Water Works undertaking. The minutes were then agreed tr.). div.head: ACCIDENTS AT LIVERPOOL DOCKS.
div.p: ACCIDENTS AT LIVERPOOL DOCKS.
A MIRACULOUS ESCAPE.

Numbers of persons have lost their lives, or been maimed and prevented fretn earning a livelihood through accidents at the Liverpool docks. Scarcely does a week pass without one or two inquests being held. The ambulance corps is engaged with a yearly average of oue accident per day caused in or about the docks. And many of the poor fellows who are the vic- tims end their working life from the hour of the mishap. How many of the persons who lose their lives might be saved, and how many of those who are maimed for life might be made whole and strong again? Doctors can set bones and amputate limbs, and do much with ordinary, diseases and fevers. But there are many cases where lie is hanging by a thread, doctors cannot strengthen this vital thread, and life passes away. About two and a half years ago, on the Dock Estate at the North 'End of Liverpool, a blacksmith named Pritchard, work- ing on a vessel in the dock, fell 16 feet into the hold. When picked up he was conveyed to Bootle Hospital and There examined. Several of his bones were broken. He had received an injury to the spiae which set up paralysis. In the sixteen weeks in which he was con- fined to the hospital Mr. Pritchard was unconscious for a month, and was kept in a water-bed. At the termina- tion of the sixteen weeks he was discharged as an incur- able paralytic ; and shortly afterwards one of the sur- geons who had atteuded him lectured upon his case as one of the most extraordinary and hopeless he had known. But at the present time Pritchard is almost as strong as ever he was, and is again at work. A few days ago a Liverpool correspondent called upon Mr. J. H. Pritchard at his home, 165, Boundary-st., off Stanley-road, Liverpool, and was told how the remark- able recovery had been brought about. Mr. Pritchard's home is a small shop, and when the reporter entered, the bell was answered by a strong healthy-looking man,who marched into the room with a firm, sprightly step.

_ " Is Mr. Pritchard in ? " _ "Yes, I am Pritchard." "But I thought you were paralysed.', Mr. Pritchard, having offered the reporter a seat, ex- plained the apparent miracle. "I spent twelve months at home," he said, "per- fectly helpless. My limbs remained lifeless and useless, and courage failed me. I changed from one learned doctor to another. But the doctor who told me I was incurable spoke with a knowledge of what was to come. I lost hope of ever getting well again ; I began to get utterly weary of life. This continued until a few months ago, when.what I consider to be the most blessed hour of my life occurred—the hour when I accepted the recommendation to try Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People. They renewed my life and strength and happiness. You can see that lam strong and well again ; you can see that I am not misleading you or exaggerating the remarkable character of my cure. From the time I commenced to take those pills I began to grow stronger. I have got back to work and the doctors who attended me are amazed. So are the pe )ple who come to 900 Tll9. They ask me how do I account for my cure. I can only assure them that Dr. Williams' Pink Pill are the sole cause of my recovery. The Pills have not only put life into my dead limbs, bat they have driven from my joints the most cruel rheu- matic pains from which it is possible to suffer. I have used all sorts of things for those pains ; but they re- mained until I commenced taking the Pills, and thee they gradually vanished. I tell you earnestly and sin- cerely that I owe my life to Dr. Williams—nothing but Dr. Williams' Pink Pills have cured me."

div.head: MINERS' FEDERATION.
div.p: THE MINERS' FEDERATION.

The annual Conference of the Miners' Federation com- menced at Birmingham on Tuesday. The President (Mr. B Pickard, M.P.) in his opening address said that in 1893 the miners passed through one of the most severe ordeals it was possible for any body of workmen to ex- perience. Their great fight ended satisfactorily to them, but the ending of the wages difficulty consequent upon the resumption of work at the old rate of wages did not finally close the chapter upon that question. The forma- tion of a Board of Conciliation created much discussion, and many difficulties had to he removed. Th owners' demands in 1893 were never got rid of until the decision arrived at by the Board in July last. He thought the miners in the Federation ares were to be envied under that agreement, and that the securing of a minimum rate of wages -was one of the greatest strokes of business that had ever been achieved in trade-union matters. The Parliamentary action taken hr the Federation in 1894 had been rather extensive, especial's' in regard to the Eight Hours and Employers' Liability Bills. Great opooSitiOn wva offered to the former measure, and such men as Mr. Alfred Illingworth, Mr. H. J. Wilson, Mr. J. T. Brunner, Mr. Shaw-Lefevre, and Air. John Morley would most certainly assist in wrecking the Liberal party If the Government listened to what they had to say. In ; the afternoon a resolution was adopted in favour of the reintroduction of the Employers' Liability Bill without the contracting-out clause, and afterwards the Confer- ; ence discussed proposals for equalising the entrance fee and contributions in all the districts of the Federation. The business of the annual Conference of the Miners' Federation was continued at Birmingham, on Wednes- day. It was resolved that, with a view to assist in the promotion of strict terms of equality between capitst and labour, public bodies, such as town councils, in all coal contracts which they may enter into should allow no exemption from the fulfi'ment of such contracts on account of any stoppage consequent upon ant' attempt to reonce wanes. The Conference fl fterwards considered anew Eight Hours Bill which had been drafted by the instructions of the Executive Committee. It was a similar bill to thatof last rear, with the addition of the MIT.' Secretary's amendment providing that penalties should he impoted on miners as well as on masters in eases where an offence against the Ant was committed. A resolution was adopted urging that the hill should be pushed forward with vigour at the opening of Parlia- ment. A resoliition protesting against the compolsorr es'Ahlishment of Arbitration Boards was agreed to uni- mnusly.

div.head: RUNCORN SAVINGS' BANK.
div.p: RUNCORN SAVINGS' BANK.
ANNUAL MEETING.

Tnt, trustees an.i ilia ii:*4-rs of the Runcorn Sayings' Ba ,k h or nmin.iin•-rtin4 on Monday afternoon. Mr. J. J.P., occupied the chair. and there were also present: Messrs. James Flandley,J.P.,Thoinss Handley, J.P., J. Simpson, F. A. Lake, T. Wright, W. Hankinson and W. Handley (.ctaary).

div.head: ACTUARY'S REPORT.
div.p: THE ACTUARY'S REPORT.

Mr. Wm. Handley. the actuary, in his report, said that the total separate transactions over the counter, inclusive of deposits, withdrawals, transfers, stock por- chases and dividends thereon. numbered 3,480, the cash turnover being £18,803 2s. Id., whinh, with the stock purchases, dividends and transfers amounting to £1,114 84. Id., brought up the total business to £19,717 103. 2d. The stock account had largoly devel- oped during the year, the increase being £1,050. Tile dividends credited and paid to delyisitors having corres- pondingly increased from £32 193. 10i. to £BO 183. 101 During the yearseveral visits had been paid to the hank by the officials of the Saving's Bank Inspection Commit- tee, under the powers of recent acts of Parliament, and the books of accounts and the system of audit examined by them. They recommended that the bank should en- deavour to extend its usefulness by increasing the hour; of business, and by making widely known the increase of limit now allowed by Act of Parliament, viz., de- posits from £3O to £5O, and in investments from £lOO to £2OO within the year, up to a maximum of £2OO de- posit, and £5OO stock. The new arrangement came in- to force in October last, arid had resulted in some addi- tional annual expenses having been caused for manage- ment, but if the increase of business Was commensurate With additional facilities afforded, it was to he hoped that any anxiety on that account would not arise. The highest rate of interest allowed, was credited on all de- posits, namely, 2per cent. At the close of the bank year there were 1,122 open accounts, as follows : per- sonal depositors 1,054, penny banks 1, charitable socie- ties 15, friendly societies 81. The amount owing to these depositors was £31,328 ss. 51., against which the National Debt Commissioners held £30,928 Os. 7d., and the treasurer for current requirements £493 4i. Bcl., showing a surplus of assets over liabilities of £92 193. 81 The auditors had frequently been in attendance and certified to the correctness of the accounts. In accord- ance with a general suggestion of the Inspection Com- mittee these gentlemen had arranged to attend still more frequently during tho year. Since the close of the bank year over 400 pass books had been presented at the counter for the entry of the interest. These had been com- pared with the ledger and found correct. The past year had been noted as one of severe local commercial depres- sion but as there were expectations of a brighter future it was hoped that with the increase of facilities both in hours, and amount of deposit, the bank might share in the looked-for good time and increasingly maintain its position as one of the permannit and flourishing institu- tions of the town of Runcorn.

div.head: THZ AUDITOR'S REPORT.
div.p: THZ AUDITOR'S REPORT.

The auditors, M-i;sr;:,-1. U. Salkeld.Eiward Marwood, Williamson, and C. Pownall reported that they had audited the various accounts and found them all correct The bo.ks had been well and accurately kept by the actuary and they clearly showed the amount due to every deposition.

div.head: THR REPORT &HOPPED.
div.p: THR REPORT &HOPPED.

The Chairman moved the adop-tio-n—o.! the report, and in doing so said it was satisfactory to them to know that they were progressing, and that the b.dance was on the right side. They were in a Nourishing condition, and notwithstanding the had times they were able to pay their way and have a tolerably good surplus. He re- membered it was said that if they could get something like £20,000 invested they would be able to pay their way, but they had now nearly £31,000 in the hands of the National Debt Commissioners, which, together with the amount in the hands of the treasurer, exceeded £31,000. This gave them a good margin to provide for expenses. He hoped that the present year would be a more prosperous on, and that their annual report would show that there were persons in Runcorn who were thrifty and willing to avail themselves of an institution such as that.—Mr. J. Handley in seconding the proposition, said that the present satisfactory results had not been arrived at without considerable labour on the part of those connected with the Savings Bank. He and the Chairman had been long connected with the bank, and he could remember when the business was very small. He thought great credit was due to all who had assisted in the bank's development.— The report was adopted unanimously.

div.head: VOTES OF THANKS.
div.p: VOTES OF THANKS.

Dr. McDougall, in moving that the best thanks of the meeting be given to, Mr. Simpson for his services as treasurer, said it would be the wish ef the depositors, and all those associat,d with the bank, that Mr. Simpson should be spared for many years to fulfil the office of treasurer.—Mr. Lake seconded, and the proposition was carried unanimously.—Mr. Simpson acknowledged the compliment, and said he believed it was almost 40 years since he was appointed treasurer of the hank. He was very glad the bank had gone on increasing, and that the prospects were so favourable.—Mr. T. Handley moved a vote of thanks to the auditors for their careful audit of the bank's business, and also moved that they be re-appointed for anGther year at the same salary.—Dr. McDougall seconded, and the motion was carried.—Mr. Wright proposed a v*to of thanks to the Chairman (Mr. Brundrit) for his ‘services. They knew that the bask was in good hands whilst he was the president.—Mr. Hankinson seconded, and the motion was adopted unanimously.—The Chairman, in reply, said he took great interest in the bank, and had been a depositor since 1847. Be hoped, as long as he was spared,te take his share in the management of the bank.

div.head: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.

On Tuesday, a sitting of this court was held at the Sessions House, Runclrn, before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes. There were :or hearing 45 original plaints, sie default summonses, and two judgment sum- monses.

CLAIM AGAINST A FRODSHAM CORN MERCHANT. —The Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Com- pany brought an action against James Edwards, corn merchant, Fmdsham, for demurrage. £l5 73. 61. was claimed for demurrage on 60 sacks of oats at Moles- worth, in Septemb,.r, 1893, and in respect of 100 sacks at Warrington, in March last. With reference to the first item the plaintiffs alleged that the sacks were hired by the defendant himself, but in the Warrington case the sacks were first received in the name of Johnson, who sold the oats in the sacks to the defendant. Edwards after the sacks had been lying at Warrington for six weeks, sold the contents to a George Edwards, of Ruabon, and the claim was in respect of this period of six weeks as the usual rate ofd. per sack per weAr. It was contended on behalf of the plaintiffs that it was the custom in the corn trade at Warrington for the person to pay to whom the pr-duce was transferred so long as he allowed it to remain on the company's premises. The defendant denied all liability, and said he did not hire the sacks in the Molesworth claim. His Honour, in giving judgment, said he was not satisfied that in the Molesworth claim the defendant hired the sacks, and as it was admitted he did not do so in the Warrington ton claim the plaintiff wo Id be non-suited. He was of opinion that the proper claim by the plaintiff was for warehousing the sacks.

"MEN ARE DECEIVERS EVER "-AN OLD SAYING VERIFIED.

On Monday morning, at the Borough Police Court, before the Mayor (chairm in; and other magistrates, Henry Walker and Robert Holmes Sheph'erd, last from Liverpool, were charged with obtaining from James Davies, 24. by means of a trick.—The Chief Constable stated that the complainant was James Davies, joiner and builder, 8, Fennel-street and on Friday last the prisoners came from Liverpool to Warrington and lodged lat the " British Workman," Horsemarket-street during Friday night. On Saturday morning between six and seven o'clock they went to the coffee rooms of Edward Lawson, Buttermarket-street. They there engaged a for the night and after partaking of tea they got into conversation with Mr Lawson. They asked him if he knew a builder suitable for erecting a corn-mill which they wanted to make in the house lately occupied by Mr. Dunn, at Latchford, representing themselves to be agents for Mr. Rogers, 21, Water-street, Liverpool. Mr. Lawson referred them to Mr. Davies, the complainant, as a likely contractor. The prisoners went to com- plainant's house and said they had heard of him at a suitable man. They told complainant the same tale, which he thought was very plausible. Complainant and prisoners went tea public-house and had a drink or , two, afterwards returning. Instructions as to the alter- ations were given to Davies, when Walker saying they were a bit short, asked complainant to lent them two shillings for a while, and complainant complied. An estimate for £4 and a plan were drawn up mad actually posted to Mr. Rogers in Liver- pool. A key, about an inch and a half long was given to complainant as the one of Mr. Dunn's house door. The smallness of the key and its very ap- parent ridiculousness first arroused complainant's sus- picions, and he therefore sent word to the police. De- tective. Sergeant Monaghan went to Lawson's rooms, and there found the prisoners upstairs. He conveyed them to the police station.—James Davies, the com- plainant, gave evidence, in which he supportel Mr. Hunt's statement.—The chief constable (Mr. Hunt) applied fora remand of two days as be had reason to the prisoners were wanted at Liverpool. The Bench ac- cordingly acceeded to the application. On Wednesday morning, before Mr. John Fairclough (chairman), Mr J. H. Fleming and Mr. J. Cieddes, the case was resumed, and the following charges added to the one detailed above :—Henry Walker and Robert Holmes Shepherd, both charged with having on the 4th inst. obtained from John Mounfield, cabinet maker, 17, Church-st. by means of a trick, the sum of 2s. 6d., his money, and by similar means and on the same date with obtaining is. in cash and stealing some members' books of the " Children's Burial Society," and a pair of stockings belonging to Edward Powell, joiner, Foundry- st. Both prisoners pleaded guilty.—The Chief Con- stable (Mr. S. Hunt) stated to the magistrates that they had not been long in finding that Mr. Mounfield, the complainant, in the second case bad been visited by Prisoners on the same date and they had told him a story identical with the one in the first case, and had also prevailed upsn him to draw up an estimate and for- ward it to Mr. Rogers, of Liverpool. This done the first prisoner (Walker) begged for 2s. 6d., and on re- ceiving it handed Mr. Mounfield a key similar to the first with which to enter Mr. Dun's house. In the third case Mr. Edward Powell, joiner, Foundry-st. was visited by prisoners at his residence, 13, Edward-qt. On the day in questigp they came to him and Walker said, " We have been I.ecommended to you and we want a corn mill making for a gentleman in Liver- pool," giving the latter's name, etc. They were asked inside and had had some beer with Mr. Powell. While conversing they also visited the " Blue Back,' and the " Higher Angel," public houses, afterwards returning to complainant's residence. Here, Walker (who was the chief spokesman) told Mr. Powell that he had come without a waistcoat and asked him to lend him one. Mr. Powell found prisoner a waiscoat and also lent him a shilling. A key in all respects similar to the two others was handed over to him with corresponding directions. While Mr. Powell was upstairs finding the waistcoat the prisoners abstracted the books produced from a pocket in a coat hanging up there. These articles were afterwards discovered in the pris- oner's bed at Mr. Lawson's. The stockings pro- duced) were afterwards discovered to be missing from Mr. Powell's house, and were found in Walker's pos- session. Mr. Powell visited Mr. Dun's house and found that the key would not fit any door. When charged with these offences at the Police Station the prisoners said " We have nothing to say to any charge." Continu- ing Mr. Hunt said the men were wanted by the Liver- pool police and he had received the following telegram from the Chief constable there.—" Your letter of 6th re Henry Walker. If acquitted on your charge please detain him, and Shepherd wanted here on similar charges. Please write—Head Constable, Liverpool.—The men are wanted in other places and every where the corn-mill tail has been used. Bth prisoners were committed to gaol for one month on cach charge, (3 in all.)

The usual meeting of the above on Sunday afternoon was not quite bo well attended as usual, owing perhaps, to the fact that there were other attractions outside on that day; but the matter submitted at the service was quite in keeping with the excellence of those gone be- fore. Mr. Rayley was chairman, and he gave a brief address. The speaker was Mr. W. Gosling, of Manches- ter, who gave an effective sddress on the " Sentiments prevailing at the present season, dealing with the universality of wishes, universality of benevolence, and universality of hopefulness." Miss Roberts sang as a sola, "When the children pray," with violin obligato by Mr.Pearson,with her accustomed sweetness._

div.head: WYCLIFk CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH:
div.p: WYCLIFk CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH:

There was a large attendance at the above church on Sunday, at both morning and evening services. Special New Year's addresses were given by the Rev. J. Yong° (pastor) and the one in the morning was specially devoted to young people. At the conclusion, the annual distribution of bibles was made to the members of the Pastor's special class who had attained the age of 15 dur- ing the preceding year. 42 candidates this year presented themselves for the honour. Considerable attention was manifested by the congregation at the evening service, when the Pastor preached an eloquent sermon on the Wycliffe Church motto for 1895, "Redeeming the Time." BOLD-STREET WESLEYAN CHURCH PEOPLE'S

div.head: SERVICE.
div.p: SERVICE.

Mr. G. Bailey presided over the usual Sunday afternoon meeting of the above on the last occasion. After the lef son had been read and prayer offered, the orchestral band played a selection from Rossini's "Stabat Mater." The Chairman then called upon the Rev. G. D. Mason, who said he was glad it had fallen to his lot to address them on the first Sunday in the New Year, and with his own lips and from his own heart to wish them all God's best gifts and richest blessings throughout the year upon which they had just entered. He wished to point out several fundamental principles wkich must be observed in order that the present year might be what it ought to be. First of all, they must be right with themselves. It was necessary for them to examine themselves from time to time—in relation to their thoughts, to their words and to their habit of speech and 'action. Secondly, they must endeavour to be right in their relationship to others, not only by doing them no injury, but also by doing them all the good they possibly could. Their duty had been well expressed in the words of the prophet Micah, "to do justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God." This relationship should exist not only to those who were good to them, but even to their enemies. In addition to being right with themselves and with others. they must be right in their relationship to God. They must hive pardon for the past, peace for the present, and a knowledge of Christian hope; and having these, they would experience" the peace of God which passeth all understanding." Let them take as their guide Him who would never slip, never sleep, and never forsake them. Mr. Fieldhousfs gave an excellent rendering of Gounod's "Nazareth," to the orchestral accompaniment, and a few well chosen remarks by the chairman brought the service to a close.

div.head: UNEMPLOYED. RIOTS IN NEWFOUNDLAND.
div.p: THE UNEMPLOYED. RIOTS IN NEWFOUNDLAND.

Telegrams from St. John's, Newfoundland, describe serious rioting on the part of the unemployed. Being refused admission to the• Legislative Ckamber,they burst the door open, but wero eventually cleared out by a reserve of police. The crowd then proceeded to Govern- ment House, and reiterated to the Governor their demand for public relief to save them from starvation. The Governor declared that he was powerless to act without the co-operation of the Ministry, but the Premier afterwards declared that employment would be provided within three days. In the end, the stores of Messrs. Dudcr and Co. were attacked, but the n.ob was beaten off by the police with drawn swords. Bluejackets have been landed.

div.head: -to-- THE WEATHER-ICE ACCIDENTS.
div.p: -to-- THE WEATHER-ICE ACCIDENTS.

In many. parts of the country snow fell heavily on Monday. 'The railway traffic in the north of Scotland was stopped by the drifting snow. The frail character of the ice formed by recent frost has caused the loss of many lives. At Blackburn, on Sunday, the lake in the Queen's park was crowded with people. A large sheet of ice gave way, and over 60 people were immersed. So far as is known, only one person was drowned. Two youths were drowned on Saturday at Fenton, Stafford- shire, and on Sun lay fatal accidents occurred at Ches- ter, Long Sutton, and Stairfont, near Birnsley. On Monday a man named Young was drowned at Earls. wood, Surrey, while trying to rescue a boy who had [taro into a pond while skating. The boy was saved. Two young men fell through soin, ice at Shelton, Wor- c!stershire, on Monday, and were both drowned.

a. TB navigation of the Ship Cans Navigating the Cana by the Anchor Line steamer. l. - " Hispania " was an event of some importance. The "Hispania" is a vessel of 3,380 tons register—the largest vessel which 110 passed along the canal. Her voyage was notable, too, from the fact that she was the first of a regular line of steamers which will, under a eon- tract, carry cotton goods between the new port of Manchester and Bombay. The passage of this big boat along the Canal,has, therefore, been subject of unusual interest amongst the very numerous people who are interested in the fortunes of the great waterway. If this vessel could safely navigate the Canal there is no reason why others of a similar or smaller tonnage should not, and the old taunt that the canal is only fit for barges is effectually disposed of. we can now speak after the event. Tb 4 " Hispania " has been to Manchester and backt.J and it has safely navigated the Canal' This fact can be vouched for on tlas unimpeachable ,:testimony of a not tek favourable witness. The Liverpool rivals 01 Manchester were evidently deeply interested .ini the affair, and a representative of the " DadY'tg Post " appears to have been on board the " pania " and gives an elaborate account of the voyage outward. The vessel left the inland pors on Sunday morning, and on Sunday night she was at the Albert Dock, Birkenhead, wher e she was to comple to her loading. There were nn casualties to report—though we are told that the ship did receive a bump at Mode Wheel, and 8 slight graze somewhere else—and the newspaPer, man was, therefore, forced back upon the cast's' conversation of the seamen on board, in order t 4: have his fling at the Canal. "It is all very well! said one authority, when the "Hispania " was in the neighbourhood of Runcorn, "to „talk of tW4 big ships passing here ; it could not be done or a! other points—it could not be done, and, no seaman who knows his business wont(' attempt it." "As for ships of large ton' nage," declared the same oracle, "passing eac,,11,. other at full speed, as was originally intended, I* is a total hallucination." But, apart from this idle gossip the passage of the " Hispania " not aftord any consolation to those Liver Pan" people who think that the Canal threatens the maritime supremacy of their world-famed eitYd The vessel undoubtedly reached Manchester an afterwards safely returned into the Mersey with substantial cargo stowed away, and that in its'!" is a fact which signifies much. When shill such as this Anchor liner once get into the waY '2 s reaching Manchester, the most sanguine drown of the promoters of the canal are in a fair way fDir realization.

The HE T question of how to deal with • Unemploed, the unemployed seems to become more and more urgent every day. This is more than a local, it is even more than a national question, for the statemen of almost every civilised commnnity have to face the problem in one way or another. It is not only in densely-populated England that the pinch is felt; there are hundreds of thousands of unemployed in America, and in some of the English colonies they from time to time demonstrate their Presence in a forcible fashion. Amongst the latest intelligence is the news from New- foundland of a serious riot under the pres- lure of which the Government has instituted relief works. In England there has, fortunately, been no lawless outbreaks—not recently at all events,—hut it is none the less certain that the number of unemployed workmen in many cen- tres of populations has reached serious propor- tions. The evil results of the want of employ- Mont are only too apparent, but it is not easy t o find a satisfactory remedy.

By OUR RUNCORN CORRESPONDENT. The streets of Runcorn at the present time bear Painful testimony to the fact that, we have in our Midst a large number of unemployed. That there !Are numbers of unemployed men is generally over- looked, when work is in full swing, but with the c.ssation of employment at the Chemical works in ~‘ne town there has been quite a marked addition ;0 the number. Groups ot able-bodied men are to 09 seen wandering aimlessly about the streets,many of.them feeling the pinch of poverty. They are '4llling, yea anxious, for work, but are unable to rllocure any. The winterly weather, too, is accen- .ating their discomfort. Their wives and children .'re in abject poverty, and the sufferings daily borne , an untold tale. The local relief committee are , 42,',ng what they can to relieve the distress, by the ""ng out of tickets for the supply of food, and the Y large number of applicants testifies to the 1 Vnount of distress in the town. But the funds at ttla disposal of the committee large as they are, ii,a,nics to the generosity of Mr. Brunner, M.P., will, itt'ne stoppage continues much longer, be inadequ- _ meet the requirements. Already numbers 0t children are being kept from school through Want of clothing.

For some years now,owing .;_tne time fixed for the meetings of the Board and tor the holding of committee meetings prior to 47,930ard meeting, in that outlandish place known b°4,..putton Workhouse, the members of the Board ve found it very convenient to have dinner pro- or them there. The number of diners has, rio B,l'er, increased of late, and as more accommoda- to tl 18 required, the Dining Committee proposed th e.aPpointed was to consider the matter. During e disc • i Amnon t was stated that the charge of one Ibin• g each had previously paid all expenses, but ot.:Farr doubted whether it had done so lately, ng that the members now dined more luxuri- than they used to do. div.head: RUNCORN MEN.
div.p: RUNCORN MEN.

_ It is now feared that several Runcorn men lost their lives at sea, during the great storm which raged on Friday and Saturday. December 21st and 22nd. It is supposed that the " Enterprise " which left Milford Haven, bound for Runcorn,on the night of the 21st ult, foundered during the burricane,and that all hands have been lost. One of the crew was Runcorn youth, 17 years f age, named Laurence Peacock, son of Captain Peacock, of Lord-st., Run- corn No tidings have been received regarding the "Betsy Nichol," of Rancorm, which was in charge of Captain Roberts, and it is also believed that she has gone down with all on board.
