UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH, RUNCORN. The first quarterly meeting of the Young People's Society of Christian Endeavour, connected with the above-named church was held on Tuesday night in the Ellesmere-street schoolroom, when a tea was provided, and fruits served during the evening. A musical programme was submitted, glees being rendered by the glee party connected with the Society and a solo sung by Master John Holford. Addresses were delivered by Mr. A. Clarke, and Mr. F. Barker. The pastor of the church, the Rev. J. Stafford, presided. It was announced that the number of members of the Society now amounted to seventy. There was a large attendance and a pleasant evening was spent. COLLIER'S BREAD is the best money can buy.—Advt. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD. The meeting of this board was held on Wednes- day afternoon. Mr. Morris occupied the chair, and there were also present : Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Mr. Thos. Handley, J.P., Mr. Mellor, Mr. Coleburn, and Mr. Salkeld (secretary). The report submitted by the secretary showed that the interments for eight months to November 25th amounted to 201, and for the corresponding period last year 362, decrease 161. The fees received for the same period were .£l9l 9.. Bd., against .£334 18s., being a decrease of £143 Bs. 4d. The report was considered very satis- factory. Accounts amounting to .£3 9s. 3d. were passed for payment on the motion of Mr. Coleburn, seconded by Mr. T. Handley. RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD. _

On Tuesday evening a meeting of this Board was held in the Board-room at the Town Hall, Run- corn. Mr. J. Pritchard occupied the chair,and there were also present—the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, Rev. Dr. Gastaldl, Dr. McDougall, Mr. T. Handley, J.P., Mr. E. Imison, J.P., Mr. S. Taylor. J.P„ and Mr. G. Moss (clerk). It was decided that the Chairman and the Rey. Canon Wood should form a deputation to attend the annual meeting of School Boards, but to pay their own expenses.—The Clerk read a statement showing that arrears to the amount of .£2 3s. were owing to the Board by three parents whose children were in Blind,and Deaf and Dumb Institutions.—Dr. McDougall strongly com- mented upon the fact that the matter had not pre- viously been brought before them, and that the parents had been allowed to accumulate such large arrears.—The Clerk stated that the arrears had acclimulated quite recently,and were largely due to the distress in the town.—ln reply to questions, the Clerk said the Board was contributing to the maintenance of four children in blind and deaf , institutions, and the cost was about £2l each.—Dr.l Gastaldi said it would be useless to take the parents before the magistrates at the present time. , They really could not pay the money.—The Clerk stated that two ot the persons who were in arrears had been receiving relief.—lt was decided that pressure should be brought to bear upon the parents for the payments of the amounts due.—This con- cluded the business. ST. PAUL'S BIBLB CLASS, RUNCORN. On Wednesday evening the annual tea meeting in connection with this class wee held in Brunswick Wesleyan schoolroom. Over 100 persons sat down to tea. The decoration of the room had been carried out by the following :—Mr. G. Hayes, Mr. T. Leach, Mr. Noncollis, and Mrs. Nancollis. The 'after proceedings were commenced with devotional exercises, conducted by the Rev. J. H. Tite. The election of officers was then proceeded with. Mr. J. D. Tones proposed, Mr. A. Wilding, and J. 4. Smith. Messrs. Wilding, Crosby,Greenwond, Millington and S.:Coventry were re-elected visitors. Le Couteur, the miss- ing engineer of the tug Liberator, and Captain Woodhou,e, of the dredger,Barry, both of whom are supposed to be drowned, have been fruitless. THE POLICE STATION AT RUNCORN. ! A sub-committee appointed by the Standing Joint Police Committee of the Cheshire County Council met at the Runcorn Police Station on Monday, to consider the Government Inspector's report en his recent inspection, in which lie stated that the cells and offices were inadequate, and that further pro- vision should be made. The Runcorn magistrates present were Mr. J. Brundrit and Mr. T. Speakman, and Colonel: Hammersley, chief constable, wa.; also present. The police station was inspected, and sug- gestions were made, but no definite scheme was de- cided upon. NEWSBOYS' TREAT AT RUNCORN._

The newsboys of Runcorn were on ,Thursday evening, through the generosity of Mr. and Mrs. Henry Darlington, of the Railway Hotel, provided with a treat. A substantial supper, consisting of rabbit pie, hot pot, mince piece, were provided, and it is almost needless to state it was clone full justice to. Tea and coffee were also supplied, an.', on leaving, each boy received an orange. The I.,Jys expressed their thanks by hearty cheer,. TRH DISTRESS IN RIINC,sO-1.1. During the week, the applicatio,,,oc relief have largely increased, and this may be accounted for by the severe weather experienced. On Wednesday evening when the various ward committees met, the stations were surrounded by large numbers of men and women applying for relief, and the com- mittees were kept engaired until late in the evening. Meetings of the supervision and general committees were held on Thursday, when orders were distri- buted for food. The subscriptions received during the week include .£5 from Messrs. Ocklestou and Son ; .£5 from Australian Alum Company; and ..£1 Is. from the Rev. W. George. Major llazlehurst and Mrs. Charles Hazleburst have decided to contri- bute £1 weekly. The employ 6 i of the Runcorn Co-operative Society have also been contributing to the fund weekly.—A soup kitchen is to be opened at the Seamen's Institute the sum of £3 6:4. 8 1., has been collected from the porters at Runcorn docks; £2 2s. from Mr. G. Bellamy, and 10s. weekly from Mr. W. R. Wass.

RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
THE FIRST MEETING.

At Dutton Workhouse. on Tuesday, the first meeting of the District Council for the rural district of Runcorn was held. There were present : Messrs. J. Mclntyre, J. Knowles, J. Stokes, H. E. Heywood, J. M. Williams, W. Pickering, J. Weir, J. Brandreth, S. Woodward, J. P. Jones-Parry, J. Spruce, C. Rovlance, T. Wright, E. Aaron, G. Friestner, J. Parr, J. Darbyshire,W. Bradford, J. L. div.head: APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN.
div.p: THE APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN.

Mr. J. Weir —Proposed that Mr. Mclntyre he ap- pointed chairman, He thought they could not do better than propose the late chairman of the old authority. —Mr. Parr seconded. Messrs. E. Aaron, J. Darbyshire and Woodward supported, aud the motion was carried unanimously.—Mr. Mclntyre in responding, thanked the members for unanimously electiug him to the position of chairman. In tak- ing the chair, he had no doubt judging from past ex- perience, that he would have the support of all the mem- bers of the Council. He was pleased to see a great many faces of men who had worked with them there in the past. He congratulated the new members upon their appointment, and hoped they would take an interest in the work of the Council.

div.head: INQUEST AT RUNCORN. THE GRANTING OF DOCTOR'S CERTIFICATES.
div.p: INQUEST AT RUNCORN. THE GRANTING OF DOCTOR'S CERTIFICATES.

Mr. J. E. Worsley, coroner, held an inquest on'Tkurs- day morning, at the Bridgewater arms, Runcorn, on the body of an infant daughter of Thomas and Margaret Faaackerley. boatpeople. Mrs. Fazackerley stated that deceased was six weeks old. She had been ailing from birth but became worst the previous Thus.4day. She took her to Dr. Robinson's surgery on Saturday night, and saw Mr. Bankes, his assistant, who gave her some medicine. The deceased was not seen aga'n by a medical gentleman, and died on Tuesday morning. She followed the directions given by Mr. Bankes. She was taking the baby to the boat on Monday night. but when she reached Percival-lane, she saw the child was worse and returned to her mother's houses. She bad had a child before, which died from convulsions. Dr. Robinson stated that he did not see the baby in question whilst it was alive, hut he directed Mr. Bankes what medicine to give on Saturday .after hearing the symptoms of the complaint. He intended, to see the infant, but through change of address by the parents he was uuable to seo it. He had seen the child that morn- ing and in his opinion death was due to constitutional disease from birth. No did not think any treatment would have saved the child. Witness said that he m see it a rule not to examine infants at the 'surgery. There were many parents ready to bring their children to him to ensure getting a certificate in case of contingencies; they risked their children's lives in doing so. The Coroner said medical gentlemen should refuse to give a eertificate under such circumstances, and then if anything happened, have the ease brought before him, so that he could hold an inquest. That was the best way to do. Did Dr. Robinson think that the parents in the 'resent case were to blame for taking tie deeeased out? Dr. Robinson replied that if the child had belonged to parents in better circumstances it would not have been allowed to leave a warm bedroom. But the mother apparently thought the child was better,and was taking It to the boat. The Coroner said that considering the circumstances he did not think the parents were to blame. The jury concurred in this opinion, and recorded a verdict in accordance with the medical evidence.

div.head: LA.TCHFORD AMATEUR DRA.4ATIC SOCIETY.
div.p: LA.TCHFORD AMATEUR DRA.4ATIC SOCIETY.
PERFORMANCES AT THE PARISH ROOM:

A very great surprise was in store for all those who at- tended at the Parish Room, Latchford, on Tuesday and Wednesday evenings, when the Latchford Amateur Dramatic Society gave two performances,which, for the successful interpretation of every part and the marvel- lously pleasing effect of the whole, are almost without parallel in the recollection of both Latchford and War- rington people. The object of the performances was a worthy one, namely, the augmentation of the funds of the Warrington Musical Society, whose exchequer has of late been so much in need of help. Considering that each evening the room was well filled by a fashionable and appreciative audience, which did not by any means shun the reserved seats, the pecuniary results of the project will be highly satisfactory both to the promoters and to those who will most materially benefit from it. 'rho furnishing of the different draw- ing rooms, etc., in each act, which really comprised the scenery was exceedingly tasteful. The costumes of the performers were extremely elegant and in admirable taste. The wigs etc., which were used, were supplied by Mr. Birch Browne. On Tuesday evening the programme was opened in a fitting manner, with a drama in one act, entitled " The Cape Mail " (Clement Scott). The seven characters in the piece were as follows :—Mrs. Preston, Miss Broadbent ' • Mrs. Frank Preston, Mrs. J.A. Edelsten ; Mary Preston,Miss Sylvia Broadbent; Mason, Miss Reynolds ; Surgeon-Major Hugh Marsden, M.D. Mr. Frank M. Appleton; Mr. Quicke, Mr. H. Beresford Melville ; Bartle, alr. Frank H. Crossley. The drama is based upon the following interesting and pathetic story. Mrs. Preston, a sweet-tempered blindjold lady, lives ia London in company with Mrs. Frank Preston, her daughter-in-law whose husband is in the army abroad, and Mary Preston, her daughter. News reaches Mrs. Frank Preston and Mary, that the fortner'a husband has been killed in battle and, though their own distress is very great, they determine to keep the sad tidings as much as possible from the ears of old Mrs. Preston. In the carrying out of this purpose much petty deceit is found to be necessary, such as reading aloud imaginary and hopeful letters from thelson, and attend- ing balls, dances, and other assemislies of a like nature. At this point Surgeon-Major Marsden, a comrade and old friend of the dead soldi,-r, returns home and is much grieved to hear of the light-hearted and frivolous conduct of his friend's wife and sister. He calls, indignantly, to demand an explanation, but on seeing the true cause of their conduct his anger turns to pity and sympathy for the sufferings of the two who find this deceit necessary. Becoming more distressed and unable to keep up the deception Mrs. Preston (wife of the deceased soldier) resolves to tell her mother-in-law. While on this mission Mr. Quieke' the family lawyer, comes in with the news that Frank Preston is alive and brings a re-assuring letter from him. Fortunately Mrs. Preston had been unable to nerve herself to telling her mother-in-law of her son's supposed death, and the latter comes upon the scene in time to allay the suspicions which had arisen within her mind that all was not well. The large amount of pathos and feeling which this drama gives occasion for is exceeding well expressed by those taking part and at some points the audience was visibly affected. The next item produced was an 'original comedy in three acts entitled "War to the knife" (Henry J. Byron) in which material of a gayer turn is plentiful. The different characters were taken as follows :—Mr. Bar court (a Young Married Man), Mr, H. 13,resford M./- vile; John Blunt (a Bristol Manufacturer), Mr. Finlay Dun; Nubtly (of the Cosmopolitan Coal Empc,rium),Mr. John White; Sharpus (a Detective), Mr. Frank M. Appleton ; Captain Twistleton (Unattached), Mr. Arthur Dun; Mrs. Harcourt (a Young Wife), Mrs. J. A. Edels- ten ; Mrs. Delacour (a Young Widow), Mrs. Finlay Dun; Mrs. Penson (Mrs. Hare.ourt's Maid), Miss Reynolds; Jane Trimmer tMrs. Delacour's Maid), Miss Maud Bleckly. In this piece the " plot " is composed of " dlficulties "in high life, of the usual kind. A bank is also broken, which affords a reasonable rxcuse for the arrest of one of its swindling directors—Captain Twistle- ton. For the humorous side the audience were chiefly indebted to Mr. John White,as Nubbly, the greengrocer, itc., though amusing contretemps in the acts are not in- frequent. There are three acts, two in Mrs. Harcourt's well appointed drawing room and one in that of Mrs. Delacour. Throughout the comedy the vivacity and humour of the various characters was well sustained, and the performance was of an exceptionally interesting character.

WEDNESDAY'S PROGRAMME. The second evening was in every %VA y as successful as the proceeding one, both in point of attendance and the excellence of the programme submitted. A commence- meat was made by the reproduction from the previous night, of" War to the Knife "in which the same artistes aquitted themselves with equal success. After the completion of this comedy, a comedietta in one set, " Who's to win him," by Thomas S. Williams, was inau- gurated by theraising of the curtain and consequent dis- closure of an entrance hall to a country house, in which all the events of the piece take place. There were eight characters comprising the following :—Cyril Dashwoed (A Young Officer in search of a wife), Mr. Arthur Dun ; Mr. Prattleton Primrose (A Middle Aged Bachelor of an undecided turn), Mr. W. Bede Greener; Squire Brush- leigh (A Country Gentleman), Mr. Frank H. Crossley; Rose (Brushleigh's Daughter),Miss Maud Bleckly; Sylvia (A Young Lady fond of " Sport "), Mrs. J. A. Edelsten ; Minuetta (a young lady fond of dancing), Miss Sylvia Broadbent; Musidora (a young lady fond ef romance), Miss Reynolds ; Arabella (their friend, a young lady fond of flirtation), Miss Broadhent. Briefly told, the commedietta illustrates the following wary :—Mr. Cyril Dashwood arrives, from abroad, at the house of Squire Brushleigh, with the set purpose of 'biding a wife. His arrival is not looked favourably upon by Mr. Frattleton Primrose, who had had the society of the Squire's three charming nieces and friend all to himself for sore time, and therefore he does not welcome strangers. All three nieces and their friend sionuitane- I ously fall in love with Dash wood at the commencement, and successively " bait " him, but without result, while Rose the Squire's daughter, unintentionally captivates Dashwood, with the result that the latter proposes and is accepted. While all the love-making was going on Mr. Primrose wee consumed by jealousy, and in his des- 1 pair,proposes to all the young ladies, one after another, I but is rejected with laughter and scorn. All the parts were taken with great skill, and the voung ladies espe- cially "live up to their description.' The other three performers succeeded admirably in impressing the audience by the successful manner in which they per- formed their parts. The following instrumentaliFts from the Warrington I Musical Society's Orchestra gave their services in con- tributing the musical portions of the programme :—Mr. J. B. Caldwell. piano; Mr. It H. Pearson, Ist violin ; Mr. Brown and Mr. Clare, 2nd violins ; Mr. Ward, oboe; Mr. H. Bond, violiocello ; and Mr. H. Whitftld, has. The overture to the Bohemian Girl precluded each even- ing's performance, and during the intervals between the acts a number of sparkling items, chiefly dance music, were performed. The orchestra also, played "DiDi " , on the occasion of Miss Sylvia Broadbent' skirt dance in "Whose to Win Him P"

div.p: FRODHA.M.

DESBRTER.—At Frodsham Police Court, Wore Mr. A. Thomas, on Saturday, Emmanuel Blythe, of Volunteer-street, Frodsham, pleaded guilty to being a deserter from the 3rd Battalion King's Liverpool Regi- ment Militia, stationed at. Warrington. P.C. Price gave evidence as to apprehending the prisoner, who deserted on the 4th June, 1894. The prisoner was ordered to await an escort. The first meet- ing Was held on Monday in the Primitive Methodist Chapel. On Tuesday,the meeting was helti in the Union Chapel ; on Wednesday in the Free Church, and on Thursday evening in the Trinity Wesleyan Chapel. At. the conclusion of last night's meeting the 84crament of the Lord's Supper was administered. The meetings have been well attended, and have been conducted by the various Nonconformist ministers in Frodsham.

THE LATE MR. WM COATES.

On Tuesday afternoon the remains of the late Mr. Wm. Coates were interred in the churchyard at Stretton, amid general manifestations of grief and respect. The Rev. F. W. Willis, rector of Warring- ton, officiated. Many wreaths and other floral gifts were placed upon the coffin by the relatives and friends of the deceased, of whom there was a large number present.

div.head: DARRSBIIRY SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: DARRSBIIRY SCHOOL BOARD.

A special meeting of the Daresbury School Board was held in the Board-room on Tuesday morning to appoint a mistress. for Preston Brook Infant School, when there were present—Nlr. Mawdsley' (vice-chairman),Messrs. C. %V. Phillips,John Cooper, Peter Gleave, Rev. T. Whitley, and C. E. Linaker (clerk). Two applicants for the vacancy—Miss Jebb and Miss Pountenay—presented themselves, and after some discussion respecting the qualifica- tions, &c., it was decided that Miss Pountenay be appointed and commence duties at once at a salary of £5O per annum. SEWING MACHINES, Hand £2 18s. 6d. Treadle £4 4s. with handsome walnut eover.—J. and W. DUTTON, 16 and Sankey-. _ Warrington.— Advt. WOLIKINGMEN'S GOSPEL TEMPERANCE MISSION. • In connection with the above mission the annual dinner was held in the Mission Hall, Buttermarket- st., ou Saturday night, about GO members and friends partaking of its bounties. An interesting address was afterwards delivered by Miss B. Dutton; Mr. Feartiley amused the audience by a recitation, entitled " The Seventh Rib," and Miss Dutton and Messrs J. Rigby and S. Stringer also contributed to the entertainment.—On Sunday evening the usual Gospel Temperance meeting was held, under the presidency of Mr. J. Drury. BURNING ACCIDENT.

Charlotte Hall, nine years old, residing at 9, Glasshouse-lane, was admitted to the Infirmary on Monday night suffering from severe burns to her face, neck and both hands and arms. It appears that while the mother had temporarily left the house the child began to light a piece of paper. While doing this she accidentally set her clothes on fire, and sustained the injuries stated. A man who happened to be passing at the time, hearing the child's cries, rushed in and put out the flames. The unfortunate girl was at once taken to the Infirmary where her injuries were attended to.

The Dareebury Board school was re-opened on Monday after the Christmas holidays, and the annual prizes, consisting of money and books pro- vided by the Endowment Fund,were distributed by the governors. The following governors were pre- sent :—Mr. Philip Derbyshire (chairman), Messrs. H. Mawdsley,John Cooper,and James Parr,the Vicar being absent through sickness. The following seven children had never missed a single attendance throughout the year, and'received, in addition to a medal, a prize of 54. each :—Harry Arnold, Alice Bennett,Gertrude Wright,Amy Weir,Ethel Mulkey, Frank Arnold, and Fred Weir. The following chil- dren had only been absent one half-day through sickness, and they also received ss.:—William Lockett, Charles Foulkes, Percy Wright, William Arnold, Martha Leach, Leonard Leach, and Lily Prince. Other prizes for attendance ranged from 41. to 2s. according to merit, while the prizes for marks, &c., ranged from 2s. 61. to Is. The total number of prizes given were about 230. At the ccnclusion of the distribution Mr. Cooper addressed the scholars,and the meeting was brought to a close by cheers for both governors and teachers. As usual, a holiday was given in the afternoon. Si'. PETER'S MOTHERS' MEETING. On Monday evening, the annual tea party in con- nection with the St. Peter's Mother's Meeting was given in John-st. schoolroom when about 110 mem- bers partook of an excellent tea prepared by Atesdetnee Percival, Taylor, Bamforth, Yeomans, Pearson, Richardson. and Skelland, Misses Edgar, Madeley and Brookes. After tea came a succession of games and also dancing. .Mr. P. H. Simkin played a few comic songs on his banjo, which were much appreciated; and Mr. S. Tilling ably rendered some solos on his autoharp. Miss Brookes gave a selection on the violin, accompanied by Mrs.Pendle- bury on the piano. "Jock o'ffazeldean," was well rendered by Miss Cosgrove, accompanied by Mrs. Yeomans. Mrs. Davies recited in a creditable manner a Lancashire sketch, called "Ox-tail Soup"; and the singing of "Tim Finnighan's Wake," by Mr. T. Reddish created much mirth. Mesdames Pendle- bury and Yoemans ably presided at the piano. At the conclusion the Vicar commented on the progress of the church in the parish, and he took the pros- perity of the present as an earnest of the future. Largeness of numbers, however, both in congrega- tions and in meetings of this sort, was not the only thing to be aimed at. It was a means to an end: the quickening of spiritual life, and the extension of Christ's kingdom in the hearts of all. Mrs. Per- cival then distributed n number of prizes for good attendance, the gifts being composed of parcels of cloth, &c. Three mothers: Mrs. Carter, Mrs. MaesPy, and Mrs. Warburton, won the three first prizes, not having misted one attendance. Great credit is due te Mrs. Percival and her staff ef lady workers. Tee usual votes of thanks closed a most enjoyable entertainment. ALL HoussifoLD rewire hemni.4 and marked, free of charge.—l. and W DUTTON. San kev..r., Warrington.—Advt. SATURDAY NIGHT PENNY CONCERTS. One of the most successful coecerts of the season was given in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Saturday, the roam being crowded. The chair was occupied by Councillor L Greeting. An inter- esting programme was rendered. commencing with a song by Mr. S. Hassell," My Boyhood', Love," for which he was heartily cheered. He also sang " Let me like a soldier fall." Miss Dutton, who has been a friend indeed to this movement from its inception, recited in her inimitable manner,a New Year's piece entitled " Mr. Piper," which was thoroughly appre- ciated, and was awarded hearty applause. In an equally accomplished manner she contributed two very humorous pieces, entitled •• The Kitchen Clock," and "Under the Mistletoe." Miss Pember- ton's rendering of the !song, "The Stars of , Normandie," was highly successful. She also sang ' "Waiting for the King," and on both occasions was awarded flattering applause. Mr. Adcroft contri- buted two excellently executed clarionet solos. Mr. A. Grounds was the humorist, and gave a" Musical sketch," for which he was recalled and responded. In the second part of the programme he kept the audience in continued hilarity by his comical and humorous manipulation of his life-size figures. Mr. Grounds is one of the most popular artistes who attends these concerts. Miss Toft and Mies Grounds were the accompanists on the pianoforte, and both discharged their duties in an accomplished manner. ALL HOUSIMOLD LTICIIX, hemmed and marked, free of 6 charge.—J. and W. Drriaw, Sankev.at.. Warrlnaloa.—Advi. ANNUAL TA MNEITING AT ST. 1.17100'5. On Monday evening the annual congregational e,ea in conneltion with the above church was held In the schoolroom, Liverpool-road. About 120 sat down to the meal, which was thoroughly enjoyed, after which an entertainment was given, the first portion being by the White Star Minstrels, who, in consequence of their success at a previous gathering had been invited to give their services again. The minstrels, who were under the management of Mr. G. Coggine, caused emirs of laughter by their jokes. Mr. Glover sang " Rocked in the cradle of the deep,' in a manner which earned for him loud applause. Mr. J. Wright caused SOW laughter with the singing of "Clara Nolan's Ball," aryl len O. Newton gave a good rendering of " Nnrine Maureen." Mr. Cogitins caused some diversity with his singing of " Climb up, chillen," , and Mr. Dockrey Was encored for his singing of "Mary of Argyle." Mr. A. Wallington acted as interlocutor. During the interval the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, in the course of a brief speech, said he feared the district there was drifting away from the Trinity end of the parish. He was less able to visit them than he was a few years ago, and this was because. of the increased work in Trinity parish. He was thankful for the help they had I received from people outside the parish, with- out which very little could be done, and he was pleased to see the new church prospering. It was a little cold in the winter, which no doubt interfered with the morning eengregation, hut they would not be content until they hnd made it warm and comfortable. The second portion of the enter- tainment was then commenced. All the singers were well received, seine being encored. The comic element was sustained by Mr. J. Newton, who was re-called for his singing of " Molly Riley." The programme was brought to a close by a sketch by the White Star Minstrels, entitled" Advice Gratis," the audience being kept in roars of laughter throughout. The chief characters were Dr. Snow- ball, Mr. G. Newton, and Zake, Mr. G. Ccggins. At the close the Rev. H.R. Wild said he was obliged to the performers, and especially to Mr. Conine, the manager of the minstrels, who had AO readily come forward to help him. A pleasant, evening was brought to a close by the singing of the National Anthem.

REPORT OF THE MANCHESTER AND LPi7ERPOOL DISTRICT BANNING COMPANY.

The Manchester and Liverpool District Banking CO's. report for the year to 31st December shows a net profit of £213,664 of which £lOO,OOO was taken to pay dividerd and bonus of .£1 a share for the first half of the year. For the second half a like distribution is recommended, leaving a surplus of £13,664, which it is proposed to carry to next account. The Bank's balance-sheet shows deposits amounting to £13,942,724, with a paid-up capital of £1,000,000, and a reserve fund of £1,060,000. The cash in hand, in the Bank of England and with brokers &c. at call and short notice amounts to £4,628,426, the investments to £1,849,630, and the bills of exchange and advances in current accounts to £9,793,090.

The above school was examined by Mr. Phelps, Fi.M. Inspector of schools in November last, and the managers have just received his report. All interested in the school will be glad to hear that it maintains its high reputation for efficiency. The mixed department,in charge of Mr.W. H. Stansfield and his capable staff of assistants, has gained the highest possible grant in every subject and is again classes as " Excellent." This is the fourth year in succession that the school has gained the highest mark. The subjects taught include geography, grammar, singing from note, sewing, cookery, &c. At the recent drawing examination conducted by Major Teller, the school was classed as "Excellent" in that subject. The Diocesan Inspector also gave an excellent report of the religious instruction. The infants' department,of which Miss E. Taylor is the head mistress, is also reported upon ea thoroughly efficient and as doing extremely good work. The school is very popular and its numbers are rapidly increa,ing, over 500 children being presented at the laqt examination. The managers take great interest in its welfare and desire to maintain its efficiency lin every pesgible way. ANNUAL MRETINO- OP AN ODD/FELLOWS' LODGE. The annual meeting of the Loyal Garibaldi Lodge was held at the Little Horse Shoe Hotel, on Satur- day, N.G. James Richardson in the chair, V.G. Thomas Blease in the deputy-chair. In addition to the members of the lodge there were present the following visiting brethren :—Grandneaster of the district, P.G.R. Sewell, P.P.G.M. Bramball, P.O.J. Burgess, and P.G. Kennedy from the Prosperity Lodge, Karlestown. The Sec. (P.G., T. Dickinson) presented his annual report, in which he stated that the lodge had increased both numerically and financially during the past year. The retiring grandmaster of the district (P.P.G.M. C. Bill) then presented the official medal of the lodge to P.P.G.M. Crosby, in recognition of his services to the lodge during the past year, and said it gave him much pleasure to present the medal, and hoped it would Le an inducement to other members to pass through the different offices of the lodge in the same satisfactory manner. He hoped the members during the present year would do their utmost to increase the membership of the lodge. P.P.G.M. Crosby expressed his hearty thanks for the medal, and for the kind remarks used in presenting it, and hoped he would never fail to do something for the advancetnent and progress of the lodge and order. He endorsed the last speaker's remarks in reference to young members taking an active part in the business of the lodge. The district was in a flourish- ing condition, and young men were invited to join the lodge. In time of sickness and distress friendly societies were the backbone of help and succour to the home. P.O. J. Hughes also expressed his appreciation of the services of the recipient. After some harmony from G.M.R. Sewell end other mem- bers the lodge closed at ten o'clock, a pleasant I evening having been spent. THE PIROCHTAL SCHOOL, CHURCH-STREET,

This large and important school was examined at the end of October, by Mr. E. L. Phelps, HALL, and his assistants, and a highly satisfactory report bas just been received from the department by the Rector and managers. The school is in a high state of efficiency both as regards discipline and attainments. The instruction in the elementary subjects is sound and intelligent throughout. an unusually high pitch of excellence being attained in arithmetic, particularly in the fourth standard. Grammar is not very strong in the upper classes, but geography has been admirably prepared, and the singing by note is, as hitherto, highly meritori- ous. This school is again, as heretofore, classed as" Excellent," and the highest grants have been awarded for every subject taken. as well as for discipline and singing by notes. During the first six months oc the year,the diocesan inspectors visited the echool, and after a searching examination fotwarded their report, which was also eireellent. In September Captain Royse visited the school,for drawing, and later on the Science and Art Dvartment awarded the mark "Excellent," giving the highest grants for the various branches of this useful subject. At Christ- mas, one of the pupil., Herbert Sanders, was placed at the head of those who competed for the free scholarships at the Warrington Grammar School, the examination being a very difficult one for boys of twelve years of age. There are now over 500 boys in attendance, and these are taught as an upper and lower school, by a large and competent staff of trained teachers, with Mr. Dewhurst as headmaster. Military drill for the whole of the boys, has this year been added to the long list of s übj,2cts taught'.

div.head: FATHER OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: THE FATHER OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
A POLITICAL RECORD.

In these closing years of the nineteenth eentury,when it is considered by many people to add to the reputation of any man to establish a "record," it will probably (remarks the " Times ") be interesting to politicans in particular, and to the public in general, to learn that " the Father of the House of Commons " has completed ' his " record " by ',having continuously represeated in Parliament the game constituency for a longer period than has ever been the fortune of any member of the house since its constitution in the reign of Tient! 111. The late Mr. Christopher R. M. Talbot represeWted the county of Glamorganshire from August 10, 1830, to the day of his death, January 17, 1890, a period falling a little short of 594 years. The Right Honourable Charles Pelham Villiers', who entered on his ninety-fourth year on January 3 last, completed the sixtieth year of his representation of the borough of Wolverhampton on Thursday, having been first elected for the borough on January 10, 1835. No record of his numerous elections would be complete withont mention being made of the election of 1847, when the Free Traders of South Lancashire returned Mr. Villiers 88 the colleague of Mr. Brown, the well-known Liverpool merchaut,in recognition of the triumph of the cause which he had 80 successfully championed. Although sixty years have elapsed since Mr. Villiers fought his first contest at Wolverhampton, we must lock back to the rear 1826 for his first appearance as a Parlia- mentary candidate. In the summer of that year he accompanied his brother, Thomas Hyde Villiers, into Yorkshire, and while the elder brother made a success- ful fight for the representation of Hed. on, Mr. Charles Villiers plunged at the last moment into a desperate contest as the "third man" for the representation of Kingston-upon-Hull. Fighting under the banner of Canning and Huskisson as a strong partisan of Pree Trade principles, coupled with a conviction of the just- ness and expediency of Catholic emancipation, Mr. Charles Villiers weighted himself unduly, and found himself third on the list at the close of the poll. In res- pect of this election it may probably be claimed for Mr. , Villiers that lie is the oldest surviving Parliamentary taindidate, and that no other man living foright for & }seat in Parliament so long ago as 1826.

Everything that tends to weaken our constitution and render it liable to disease is an enemy of mankind, and everything that tends to withstand the attacks of these enemies and to restore health and strength to the human system is a true friend. Among the most prominent and most dreadful. like so many generals in the attacking orces of the great enemy of mankind—death—may be mentioned the following :—lndigestion, liver complaint, nervous d,sorders, and chest affectims, while the differ- ent symptoms by which these diseases manifest them- selves may be regarded as so many sub-officers in the ranks of the enemy. When any one of these attacks us we may be certain that some of the others are close at hand. The stomach, liver, lungs, nerves, and blood, are portions of the body that the enemy is very prone to assail, and if he succeeds in maintaining his p)sition for any length rf time in arty one of them, and is not quickly expelled, he soon extends his pernicious domin- ions to other parts of the body. When the stomach is dis- ordered, we may be certain that the enemy in some form or other has gained a foothold there, and if the food be not properly digested, the blood does not receive a suffi- ciency of the vital particulars necessary to diffuse through all parts of the system in oruer to afford proper nourishment to the body. In our climate, affections of the chest are very prevalent in the form of colds, coughs bronchitis, asthma, &c. By the insidious attacks of these various enemies of man, thousands are annually laid low and brought to a premature grave. This need not be the case. The enemies can be defeated and ousted. A4' NEIGHBOURLY FRACAS. Yesterday, at the Borough police Court, before Alder- man Harrison (chairman), Dr. Gomel'', Councillor H. Roberta and Mr. J. H. Fleming, Margaret Bishop, Mission Row, Sharp-St., was charged with having wilfully damaged three windows of Mrs. Hadland'e house, Mission Bow. and Charles Bishop was charged with using threats to Mra. Iladland and her daughter at their house on Christmas day. There was a cross summons against Eliza and Edith Hadland for assaulting Margaret Bishop at the same time and place. Mr. Arthur Browne appeared for the complainant and Mr. Percy Davies for the defence.—Mrs. Hadland, Mission Row, said that on the day previous to Christmas day she complained of Mr. and Mrs. Bishop to the landlord, and on Christmas day when her daughter Lucy, from Manchester went into the yard Mrs. Bishop leaned over the wall and asked her who she was and this query was followed by some sharp language. Mrs. Bishop then caught complainant's daughter by the wrists and they had a struggle over the top of the wall, which is five feet high. She and Edith Hadland anothe daughter then interfered and tried to releaae Lucy's bands. When Lucy was released,she struck Mrs.EishoP in the face with her flst,and Edith.who was recovering from an illness fainted from excitement and was carried into the house by P.C. Marsh who now appeared 00 the Beetle. Mrs. Bishop then leaned over the wall and broke three , windows in Mrs. Hadland's house with a brush stall. A ' number of witnesses were called to support this state- ment. For the defence it was stated that the Badlands bad dragged Mrs. Bishop out of her yard by the hair of her bead and thrashed her, giviag her the black eya• with which she appeared in court. The defendatn admitted breaking the windows. Numerous witnesses were also called for the defence. In the end after the ems had lasted two hours and a quarter the defendant was ordered to pay the amount of the damage and the coat of the sursesons, g•s. A few dare age Monaghan came acrose the priagner in the" Ram-is Head," and the detec- tive kindly asked him how his wife was getting on. to which the Fisoner replied that he had not seen her for twelve months. The Stationmaster was instructed to move them away, sad the company went to a great deal of trouble to stop it. He (Mr. Fenna) came to Run- corn and saw the police inspector in Oct. last,to ask for his assistance to prevent the nuisance. Pace officers had warned the defendants, and Mr. Cook had also done so, but they defied both the police officers and the railway cfficers. As that was the first case of the kind, the Company had no desire to punish the defendants in a harsh manner. They simply wanted to stop them from frequenting the station premises.—Mr. H. A. Cook, stationmaster, stated that on the 27th November the defendants were on the approach road to the station premises. He ordered them away, but they refused to go. He had frequently told them to naive away, but they assumed a defiant attitude. He had received many complaints as to their gonduct.—Mr. Charles Jones, weighing clerk, gave evidence as to seeing the defend- ants at the station on the date eamed.—Two other young men, named Francis Collins, 12 Water-g., and Michael Moors, Mill-st., were summoned for a similar offence on the 29th November.—Mr. Fenna said that with regard to Collins he had aggravated his case, since the serving of the summons, by threatening the station- master. He asked for him to be dealt with in a different manner to the rest.—The'stationmasterspoke to ordering the two defendants away from the station premises. They refused to go. Collins had also I threatened him.—P.C. Gregory said he had warned the defendants, and had ordered them away, but they refused to go. They were there throughout the day for the purpose of touting. He had received complaints as to the filthy language used by the defendants, especially when people ref used to let them carry parcels.—Mr. Shaw (missionary) spoke of the poor circumstances the defendant Moores, was in, and said he went to the station for the purpose of earning a living.—The Chair- man said he was not at all surprised at the L. & N.-W. Railway Company summoning the defendants. From his own experience he could say that it had been an Intolerable nuisance for months and months. They defendants would each be fined the costs, and he hoped it woad be a warning to them. THEFT OF FowLs.—James Smith, of Weston. pleaded 1 guilty to having on the sth inst.at Runcorn, feloniously ' stolen a cockerel and a pullet, value 55., the property of George Marshall.—The complainant said he resided at Ashley House, Runcorn, and on Saturday between four and five p.m., he locked his fowls up for the night. He afterwards went out, and on returning at nine o'clock he bound that his hen-cote had been broken into. The staple had been drawn, and the lock thrown away. Two fowls were missing, and he identified those propuced as his property.—Sergeant Woolley said that on Saturday night be went to the prisoner's house, at Sweetman's-row, Weston, in com- pany with P.C. Morris. After they had searched the house for some titne,the prisoner pulled out the cockerel preduced from between a bed and mattress. He said he had nothing more, but afterwards drew the pullet out, saying that he took them, and was sorry for it.—P.C. Morris said the prisoner worked at Weston soapery. He corroborated the last witness's statement. On being charged with the theft,tbe prisoner replied that" he was sorry he did it, but it was all through poverty. He was very hard-up and was driven Vs it."—Superintendent Atherton stated that the prisoner had been employed half-time, and had earned 14s. or 153. per week.—The prisoner said it was the first time he had appeared in a police court, and asked the magistrates to be lenient with him.—The magistrates imposed a fine of 10s., or in default of payment 14 days' imprisonment. DaIIME AND DISORDERLY.—Richard Lewis, boatman, Runcorn, was fined 53. and costs for being drunk and disorderly in High-St. on the 7th December. FITNERIL OF THE L&TE Ala. JOSEPH DOBSON.

The deceased gentleman had been connected with the Warrington Volunteers, sea private, and many of the members paid a last tribute of resoect to his memory by attending his funeral. About 25 members of the Butchers' Association were also present, as well as several members of the old and new Board of Guardians. The ;oleo, which was a large and impressive one, left the deceased's late residence at Lumb Brook, 'at about 130. The hearse was preceded by the band of the Volunteers, which played appropriate music at intervals. The whole length of the route from Wilderspool to the Cemetery was lined on either side with spectators, and many persona awaited ate arrival of the fueeral in the cemetery. The Ray.l.Xirt'an. superintendent of the Warrington Wesleyan Circnit, was the officiating minister. At the conclusion 4 cia burial service three volleys were fired over thearave by the firing party. Hartley, J. Boscow, W. Partington, and J. Percival. SUDDEN DEATHS AT WARRING TON. REPORT OF INQUESTS. Mr. S Brighouse, county coroner, heV inquests at the Parade-room. Irlarn-at., on Tuesday, on the bodies of Jeremiah Corcoran, 19, Marsh-house-lane, who died in the evening of Saturday,and on Martin William Rhodes, "o'd Ball Inn," Winwick-road, who died from the effects of a fall, on Tuesday night, the Ist inst.—ln the case of Corcoran the first witness called was Minnie Corcoran. his daughter, who said her father Was a brewer's labourer. He was 51 years of age and an army pensioner. Witness remembered deceased coming home from his work on Satur lay list about a quarter to two. He had had some d ink and tires unable to take any dinner, but sat down in a chair by the fire. About two o'clock witness went out of the room leaving deceased In the position described, and a few minutes later heard him fall from the chair. She retorned and found him on the bearthruY, asleep,and apparently none the worse. He was wrapped up and left where he was, as being the warmest place. Neither witness or her m'ither thought there was anything serious the matter with decelvd,as he had beenin the same condition before. About a quarter to seven Dr. Hall was called in,as her father veld hardly breathe. For a quarter-of-an-hour deceased imoroved and appeared all right, hilt later in the evening he was given some mustard and water to make him vomit.but the at- tempt was uesuccetsfill. Deceased died quite suddenly about 9 o'clock. Witness was net present at the time of his death.— A Juror: I was in the same re.viment with derviasnri for 16 years —Othee jurors testified to havin known deceased for a considerable time,and all thought that he Wag a m-iat temperate man.—it,esUed, Mina Corcoran said that it was only of lite that her f +tiler had taken to drink. He had been employed at Welker' Brew. ary for 10 years.—Mary Beaman said that she lived next doer to deceased and had known him about two v. iv; He was not a man who was often tinder the influence of drink. She was called in about a quarter to seven and deceased was in the cnndition describe! by last witness. His appearance was quite natural and slim was not ' alarmed about him. An hoer after eh had returned , home, her daughter came in and rold her that deCel SS,I was dead and witness was ttstriick all of a heap."— Ernest Fox, eon-in-law of deceased, deposed to being with deceased at the time of his death and for a while, previous. Deceased, before his death. Ivo been ,1,-,r)in; soundly and witness was jokinq wi'la deceased's wife when the latter noticed that he looked pale and on wit- ness examining deceased, he found that he was dead.— The jury returned a verdict of 'Death from natural causes." In the second case—of the death of Martin William Rhodes—Alice Rhodes, wife of dereaced, was the first person to give evidence and Rho ettel that her husband was 33 years of age and resided at the " Old Ball," Winwick-road. Deceased had slipped on a piece nf scan in the lavatory and witnemi who had just felt him.heard him fall. This wag shunt 9 o'clock on the night of Tile-- day the let inst. Deceased remained in bed all night, but did not think he had broken any hsnes. HP visited tr. Hall at his Ranters, on W.idneaday, when it was found that he had broken a rib. He died on Sunday night about 11. o'elonk. The fall was quite accidental and witness had found the piece of snap sticking to deceased's shoe.—Dr. Arthur William Hall, surgeon and playsician, 39 Win wick-street stated that deceased had come to him on Wednesday evening, complaining of a pain in his left side r-sulting from a fall the previous day. The first meeting of the Warrington District Council was held on Friday at the Workhouse, when there were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Messrs. W. Houghton, J. Houghton, T. Halton, J. Johnson, J. W. Kn...iwles, T. Mather,J. Warburton,J. Dignmn, G. Thompson, J. Ball, S. Sutton (clerk), VV. Owen (surveyor), F. Kerfooc (nuisance inspector), Dr. Sephton (medical officer). The Clerk took the chair pro. tem., and read the re- turns of the recent elections to the Council.

TIIE NAME OF TME COUNCIL. The Council then proceeded to choose the name by whizth it should be known. It was pointed out that Warrington was the most cmtral town, and the Rev. G. F. Roberts moved that the name be " The Wairington Rural District Councit."—Mr. J. Houghton seconded,aud the motion was carried unanimously.
ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.

Mr. W. Houghton moved that the Rev. G. F. Roberts be chairman of the Council until April 15th. He said that Mr. Roberts was well-known as a member of Bard of Guardians, and the Assessment Committee. He had also becn chairman of the late Rural Sanitary Autho- rity.—Mr. Dignum seconded the motion, which was also supported by Messrs. J. Houghton and J. W. Knowles, and carried unanimously.— rile Rev. G. F. Roberts on taking the chair, thanked the Council for electing bina first chairman of the Warrington Rural District Couneil. He would talcs the opportunity of apologising for his absence at the last inveting of the Rural Sanitary Autho- rity when a vote of thanks had been passed to him, ft was his health which prevented his attendance, and he. now thanked the naembers for that vote. They naet that day under different circumstances to those under which they had done hitherto. They were now elected directly by the ratepayers. Before, the Sanitary Authority was elected through the Board of Guardians. That there was little breach of continuity between the two bodies was shown by what had been done that morning, when they had elected the late chairman of the Rural Sanitary Authority as their chairman. The number of members of the Council had been reduced by two, in consequence of the removal from their jurisdiction of the Cheshire township.

ELECTION OF VICE-CILkIRILLN. MI. Dignum proposed the election of Mr. William Houghton'as vice-chairman.—Mr. Thompson, as a new member, seconded he motion. He said that he had In- tended to propose Mr. Houghton as chairman, but con- sidering the Rev. G. F. Robert's long services, he had refrained.—Mr. T. Halton and the Chairman supported the nomination which was carried unanimously.—Mr. Houghton briefly replied promising to assist the chair- man to the best of his ability.

TIME AND PEACE OF MEETING. The Chairman said that he thought that the Council should be held a t some more central position than the Workhouse, (Flear,hear.) He thought that they might meet at Bewsey Chambers.—Mr. Knowles said that the majority of the Council was compo.ed of farmers and therefore it would be better to hold the meeting on a Wednesday, when they were in town. After some further discussion, Mr. Knowles moved, and Mr. Mather seconded that the Council meet in Bewsey Chambers at two o'clock, after the first meeting of the Board of Guardians in each month.—Tne motion was carried unanimously.

He was opposed to the Borough extension.—Mr, W. Hough- ton said that it was very awkward to have to unsay what he had said. I have scarcely ancthinz t gas' this wk about local football, for .' Jack ?rot" ruled suurome in the War- rington district, and he was successful in cancelling; all football matc'ina. He did the same at lllverston also, and thus provent..d Warringt-ra from making the long journey to that place.

There have b,,en no rntte—he-47-luring the preavnt year in either the first tr "A" teams have taken hart,and thererore the next time they appear before Warrington " cate," they ought to tio wiahed a Happy New Year, The frost his eArried all before it sines the new year came in, and It may prevent a mat'th to-day.

To-day—weather permitting—the first team will journey to Rochdale to plty the St. Clements of that town and Warring-An will he represente Iby the follow- ing team : Boscow, full back; Barber, Fieeanm, Moores. and Burton, throequarters ; Bate and Nevins. half hacks; Turner. Jolley, D tkin. Taylor, Barrett, S tvage, •Ind flouelton. Tne teams hay' not met for two Years, hut previnualy, victory generally lay on the side of Warrington. It most not be forgotten however that the Rochdale St. Clements have like the Rochdale FI-nmets, beaten Oldham this season, although Oldham were minus all their famous backs at the time.

The A tram, shnuld the ground he fit, will antagonise the S. Clemonts A, and ought to score rim easy victory. Our A team, however, requiries a little rnusine un, and will certainly have to play hetter than it has during the past few mstehes, or the record will not read very well at the close of the seasm.

I notice that England heat Wsles at Swansea on Sat- urday, and are thus one pin ts the go 3d in the fight for the international championship. England appear to have an ideal set of forwards, for they can play in thp:. three-coarters style when it is neCessary. They COM- pletely overpowered the Welsh forw irds during tha latter portion of the aims. It is very singular that such a powerful te-on can be obtained, practically all trom the South of England Oohs. and yetin club matches,the lnorthern teams almost invariably win. This is a fact

at needs a lot of explanation. It was in the forwards ast year that England lost their math with Ireland, a nd here will be some curiosity as to how the present f or- wards will shape against the Irish eight.

The frost does not affect the Association code as much as the Rugby, although almost al association matches in Warrington district were cancelled on Saturday. The matches between clubs in the first division of the League were, however, played without exception, and some startling results were witnessed. Everton, for instance, were beaten by Wolverhampton Wanderers by 1-0, although everyone expected the boot to be on the other leg. N 'Us Forest also showed that their victory over Sunderland a few weeks ago was no fluke, for they went to Sunderland, and succeeded in drawing with the " team of all talents."

Small Heath had been doing pretty well in the League,but on Saturday they went to Blackburn to play the Rovers, and received the biNest League beating of the present season ot 91. Liverp.ol seem to " improve worse," and were lseaten by Sheffield Wednesday on Saturday by 5-0. Altogether the winning teams had a good time of it on Saturday, for they scored no less than 27 goals to their opponents 7, and of these seven, four were scored by West Bromwich Albion.

div.p: "CAPITA.'" CHAT.

I hear on excellent authority that an energetic attempt will be made to induce the Conservative party leaders to nail bimetallism to their banners. Mr. Henry Chaplin, who now asserts that the only possible cure for agricultural depression is to revert to the double standard, is moving heaven and earth to bring this about. There are difficulties which may prove insuperable. Mr. Balfour is of course already a strong bimetallist, and Lord Salisbury is said to be practically a convert. But. unless Mr. Goschen is to be shunted, he will undoubtedly block the way, and there are other influential members of the Tory party, as well as Liberal Unionist?, who may prove intractable, Still, Mr. Chaplin and those who are acting with him will not be ,ousily discouraged, and there is a growing , feeling in Tory circles that by some means they will ultimately triumph.

When Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone arrived at London on Monday the old man looked splendid. He had a warmth cf colour about his face and a light of joy in his eyes that I have not seen for many years. His face was free from care, and his smile to the crowd that greeted him at Euston was one of beam- ing kindliness and delight. Seldom is it permitted one to see so grand and beautiful a face and head. Mrs. Gladstone looked equally well ; indeed, she carried ber eighty-five years with a buoyant air and gallant spirit: but of the two Mr. Cladstone seemel to base the most vigour.

It cannot be said that the story of Sir William Harcourt's resignation has caused even the sus- picion of a sensation in political circles. Its word- ing was suflieient to indicate disbelief on the part of the journal which propagated it, and it was not well founded,for aisuredly the South of France is not the place where Sir William's resignation, should it ever take place, will first be known. The canard was very quickly refuted. Not only was there no confirmation at the Treasury—there was emphatic contradiction. It is the very feeblest kite ever set to fly. Its sole value is to show the direction in which the hopes of the Opposition tend.

The Prince of Wales was busy with fashionable weddings oa Saturday. He was conspicuous among the distinguished companies which thronged the churches where the marriage of Sir Horace Farqu- har and Lady Scott, and of Lord Wolverton and Lady Edith Ward, sister to Lord Dudley,took place. It was a great day for society, as well as for those who rejoice in passing visions of jewels and millin- ery,and in peeps at the cream of society. The Duke and Duchess of Fife were also at the former wed- ding, and the Duke of Teck at the latter. Amid the festivities at the Countess of Dudley's residence in Grosvenor-square, the Prince did not forge the fery different scene a few doors off, at No. O, and he coiled personally to inquire after Lord Randolph Churchill.

That Vie Anti-Parnellites have effectually split into two opposing parties is now proved by the Nationalist literature on the subject and by the platform speeches of members of the two sections. The quarrel between Mr. Healy on the one side and Messrs. O'Brien and Dillon and their friends on the other, which has at last come to a head, is one of those internal broils which will not, in the mean- time, affect the position of the Government in the House, Mr! Healy's following among the Nation- alist members is too weak to enable him to effect anything very original in Parliament, and the gulf between him and the Parnellites is too great to be bridged. Besides this, Mr. Healy and his late col- leagues have certain fundamental principles in common which they cannot renounce, and which will take them into one lobby,just as Mr. Redmond and his faithful little band must also sometimes rub shoulders peacefully with the M'Carthyites in a division. What the election may do for Mr. Healy is not a point on which anyonn can hazard a prophecy; and, even if he is enabled to form a party of his own, what he will do thereafter is quite as great a conundrum.

An attempt is being made to organise the Roman Catholic journalists and writers of London on purely denominational lines under the title of the Guild of S.S. Dunstan and Bride. The new brother- hood is being formed after the manner of the old Catholic guilds, to unite all Catholic men and women who write for the press " so that they may assist one another by mutual encouragement and advice, and advance their own work by a general dedication of it to the glory of God." The promoters disclaim any desire to use the Guild as a medium of propagandi Am, though they add : " It is of course obvious that earnest members will spontaneously do their best to correct any erroneous statements con- cerning Catholic doctrines or practices that may come under their notice." It is proposed to have a mass for members on the feast of St. Dunstan, and also an annual Mass for deceased members. Similar associations of Catholic journalists are said to exist on the Continent and in America, with which the London Guild will be placed in constant touch.

A. case which will come on early in the coming sittings, and which will create some stir if it is fought out to the bitter end, is an action brought by Mr. P. A. Chance, formerly the member for Kil- kenny, against Mr. Wm. O'Brien, the member for Cork. gr. Chance claims about £.400. the balance of a solicitor's bill of costs of over £2,000 (.£1,600 having been paid) in the famous action for slander brought by Mr. O'Brien against Lord Salisbury which was tried at the Manchester Assizes a few years ago. Mr. Chanc.'s case is that he was in- structed by Mr. O'Brien to bring this action, that being an Irish solicitor he could not bring it him- self in the English courts, that with Mr. O'Brien's knowledge and consent he employed a London firm of solicitors to carry on the proceedings,and that he has paid them their bill of costs as subsequently moderated by Sir George Lewis with the consent of both parties. Mr, O'Brien's defence is what makes the case of general public interest. Sub- stantially he says that when Mr. Chance undertook the action he looked for payment of the costs not to gr. O'Brien but to funds of the Irish party then under the control of the late Mr. Parnell, and he further says that he did not pay the £1,600 already paid in respect of the hill, and that it came out of the profits of "United Ireland." Mr. Chance tra- • verses the allegation of the arrangement for the costs coming out of the party funds, and this seems to be the real csntest between the parties.

it is now the turn of the unfortunate oyster to be made the victim of the attentions of the germ doctors, who are gradually going the round of all our articles of food, if not to frighten liP, at least to gnarl Us from the ills that flesh is heir to. If poor mortals were very squeamish they would neither drink water nor eat food, lest they should die of typhoid fever or some other disease that originates from the swallowing of microbes. We ought logi- cally and on sanitation principles to stop breathing, as the air is laden with deadly elements, and every breath is the inhalation of the seeds of fatal disease. Two or three weeks ago we were all cautioned against watercress, and to-day the medical mind has wakened up to the danger of the bivalve which has been supposed hitherto to be the greatest dainty of the epicure. Oyster beds are cultivated near towns, or in rivers laden with sewage. Therefore, while the ,ucculent bivalve lives its charined life amid the filth :and even flourishes and fattens and grows savoury upon it, the luckless mortal who devours the dainty rims the risk of sickening and dying. Every drop of the sewage water that enters the shell of the famous and costly Whitstable threatens the consumer with a doctor's heavy bill or an undertaker's ;so that the old Scriptural words, " Let us eat, drink, and be merry, tor to-morrow we die," acquire a new meaning with the discovery of bacteriology. In another fortnight we shall have a fresh crusade against some other article for which human infirmities have a need or a weakness, and if the doctors do not succeed in killing us all off by a succession of nervous terrors great will be the vitality of the human race.

INSURANCE SOCIETY CASES AT THE WARRINGTON COUNTY COU RT.
JABEZ BALFOUR WANTED AS A WITNESS.

A MISSION FOR ALDERMAN HARRISON. At the Warrington County Court,on Thursday, last week before Mr. Registrar Ridgway,J. M. Dale,agent for the Refuge Insurance Co. ,but recently agent for the Lou don, Edinburgh, and Glasgow Insurance Co., was sued by James Seddon, 131, Liverpool-road, and superinten- dent for the Warrington district of the latter Co., for £7l 63. 5d., representing money advanced on various dates in 1894, to the defendant by plaintiff. Mr. Percy Davies proseauted. Mr. Davies remarked that Mr. Jabez Spencer Balfour had formerly been chairman of the London,&c. Co. ,and he suggested that he should be sub- peened to give'evidence, as such evidence would pro- bably prove very effective. (Laughter.) He also sug- gested that Alderman Harrison, J.P., the high bailiff of the court should serve the subpoena himself, as that might have a greater influence in bringing him to Eng- land than the present proceedings of the Government. (Renewed laughter.) Mr. Davies said that in the pre- sent case, the defendant was in receipt of 303. per week, and was an unmarried man. He was at present lodging in the ro nes of the Y.M.C.A. Mr. Davies asked for an order for £1 per week. At the time the defendant borrowed the money, be led plaintiff to believe that he had rich relatives and that he would not keep him wait- ing long before the money was repaid.—Defendant denied that he was uamarried saying that he had a wife and two children. Mr. Davies asked h:m why he had described himself as an unmarried man, and whether it was not a rule at the Y.M.C.A., not to allow married men to live there. Defendant made no reply to the first question. but admitted the second. He also said that h only earned about 203. per week. He admitted that he had told the plaintiff that he nad rich relatives.—An order was made for Bs. per week. The London Edinburgh and Glasgow Assurance Co., sued James McPhillips, Rose and Crown-street,and John Glavin, Upper Bank-street, for £1 14s. 2d., money due to the plaintiff from the former as collector, and from the latter as bondman. Mraame3 Seddon represented the Company and Mr. Arthur Browne defended. Mr. Seddon produced McPhillips' accounts of moneys collected by him as collector for the plaintiff,up to August last—when he sent in his resignation—which showed a balance ow. leg to the Company of £1 144.2 d. He had also received a letter from McPhillips' who admitted owing the accounts, and promised to pay the same by instalments. —Cross-examined by Mr. Browne, Mr. Seddon said that Glavin was the guarantor for McPhillips who had re- signed of his own accord. He admitted that the defen- dant McPhillips was entitled ten times payment on an increase in the members, and that such money had been paid to him. The amount was 83. Bid and not 383. 9d. as had been stated. It was not true that he had told Mr. Glavin that McPhillips owed nothire, to the Company— His Honor pointed out .that ir it was the con- tentien of the defendant that the Company owed him the account of 83. Bid., he ought to have filed a counter claim. He promised to allow an adjournment should Mr. Browne desire it, hut could not allow costs. Mr. Browne consulted his clients, and after a short time, he informed hit-Honour that he did not think it worth while going on; as it would practically cost 43. to get 83. Bid. With regard to Glavin, Mr. Browne submitted that the Company had given time to McPhillips and thus discharged Glavin from his guarantee. His Honour said that he was not quite sure whether that was good law or not, but he was of the opinion that the plaintiffs could not sue the principal and surety at the same time. They could only sue the surety on the default of the prineipal. He therefore gave judgment for the plaintiff for £1 14s. 24. against McPhillips, and nonsuited them against Glavin.
