div.head: SAD DEATH OF A WARRINGTON
div.p: SAD DEATH OF A WARRINGTON
TRADESMAN.

THE CORONER'S INQUIRY. The death took place at his residence, Lumb Brook, on Wednesday mornieg, last week of Mr. Joseph Dobson butcher, Bridge-street, Warr- ington. He died from injuries received on the previous Saturday evening by a fall from his drag near Parr's Corner, Appleton. For a considerable num- ber of years Mr. Dabson has ben known as a butcher in Warrington and a few years ago he retired from busi- ness only to resume it again at a later date. At the time of his death he was 52 years of age. His first appear- ance in public life was in 1891 when he made a good fight against Councillor Garner in St. John's ward, being beaten by the small majority of 30 votes. Shortly after, in the earlier part of 1892. he entered the Board of Guar- dians, where, though not a very constant attender, he always expressed his opinions with characteristic shrewdness and common sense, and was not by any means a" silent member." He did not contest his seat on the Board at the recent election, owing we believe to his living out of the Union. The inquest on the deceased gentleman's remains was held on Thursday morning last week at the IN11,11)rry Tree Inn, Stockton Heath. by Mr. Worsley, coroner. Mr. J. H. Glover, of Liverpool, appeared on beh If of the Northern Accident Insurance Company, with which the deceased was insured. Miss Isabella Dobson, daughter of the deceased, was the first witness called, and she said that her father was a:butcher, and was 52 years of age. She saw him , when he came home, after the accident. He had been to Mr. Walter Darlington's, Dingle Farm, Appleton. Dr. I Fox attended him, and Dr. White was subsequently called in in consultation. Deceased's death took place on Wednesday morning. She understood her father was returning home from the farm in his drag, which was laden with straw. The straw would perhaps be 3ft. Bin. above the side of the drag. He told her that he remem- bered slipping, and that he felt the straw very uncom- fortable when he came out of the yard. Perhaps the fact that the horse had been thrashed the day before had something to do with it, as it was frightened and might have given a jump. She did not think that the horse swerved in turning the corner, and so caused her father to be thrown out. The Coroner asked if she thought the accident would have happened on a straight road ?—Witness replied that she was not in a position to give an answer to the ques- tion.—ln reply to Mr. Glover, witness said Dr. Fox was not called in ta see her father until the day after the accident. The family wanted deceased to have a doctor on the night of the accident; but he refused, as he did not think at the time, his injuries were serious. Dr. Fox said he had known the deceased for 20 years, and he had been his medical attendant for a good num• ber of years. He was called in to see him on Saturday afternoon, when he was told of the accident. The story Miss Dobson had given of the accident corresponded with the story deceased had told to witness. He found that the injuries the deceased had sustained were a , wound over the right eye, a wound on the chin, and a fraeture of the forearm. He did not think at the time that the injuries were very serious. Mr. Dobson, how- ever, got worse, and witness called Or. White in con- sultation on'Tuesd ay afternoon. Death took place onWed- neaday morning in his presence. The cause of death was effusion of the brain, and his opinion was that this was Caused by the injuries sustained in the accident. In explanation of his considering the matter not very serious at first sight, he said that in cases of injury to the head sometimes the most trifling cases were attended with the most serious symptoms at first, and the most serious cases had at first the most trifling symptoms. Mr. Dobson was a very healthy man, and also a' very sober man. FlO was told that he was a teetotaler, and he had no reason to doubt it. William Leigh, Appleton, deposed to seeing the deceased coming round Parr's corner in his drag at half-past five on the day in question, and he heard Mr. Dobson give a shout,and then fall into the road. Witness did net see the horse swerve at all. Be went to him and found that he was unccnscious. Soon afterwards a Mr. Hartley came up in his trap and witness assisted the latter to take deceased home. About the appearance of the straw and the seat on it, he confirmed the previous evidence. Mr. Glover asked Dr. Fox same questions with regard to the cause of death, and the latter stated that he had no doubt he was correct in his conclusions. He could, however, get no further without a post-mertem ex- amination, which he did not think was • necessary although it would be very interesting from a naedica, point of view. He might say that Dr. White agreed with his conclusions. Mr. Glover said he did not ask his questions on behalf of the company for the pnrpose of getting out of any claim or anything of that kind. He simply wanted to get at the facts. Further evidence was produced which corroborated all the facts mentioned above, and in the end a verdict was returned that " Deceased died on the 2nd January from effusion of the brain, caused by the injuries received from being accidentally thrown out of his drag on the 29th December." The coroner and jury expressed their sympathy with Mrs. Dobson and their family in her sad hereavemeat.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: SHIP CANAL.

A STEAMER'S MISHAP AT RUNCORN. The steamer Starlight, of Liverpool, met with a mis- hap at Runcorn, on Monday morning, whilst proceeding along the Manchester Ship Canal. When rounding the bend near to Runcorn Bridge she got too near the Mersey side and went full speed on to the bank. Three tug boats were soon brought into use, and in about an hour she was got off, and proceeded on her journey Manchester, apparently not much the worse for th mishap. EMPLOYES DINNER AT RUNCORN.

The annual dinner of the Runcorn, Preston Brook, and Anderton office staff of the Manchester Ship Canal (Bridgewater Canals undertaking) tock place on Satur- day evening, at Wilson's Hotel, Runcorn. Mr.Meadow- croft, district agent, occupied the chair,and Mr.Wiswall the vice-chair. Mr. Oldfield, the assistant manager of the Bridgewater Canals,and Mr.Boddington, jun., active partner in the Anderton Carrying Company, together with about 40 members of the staff were present. After an excellent dinner had been partaken of, provided by the landlord, Mr. Dutton, a very enjoyable evening was spent in listening to a musical programme, which was efficiently gone through. A few toasts were given, in- cluding "Her Majesty the Queen, aul Royal Family," and "The Army, Navy, and Reserve Forces."—The Chairman proposed " Success to the Bridgewater Canal undertaking of the Manchester Ship Canal Company,' which was responded to by Mr. Oldfield in very suitable terms ; and the Vice-Chairman proposed "The Port and Trade of Runcorn," which was responded to by Mr. Rawlinson. The Chairman also proposed the toast of "Success to the Anderton Company and other carrying interests identified with the Canal Company's undertak- ings," to which Mr. Boddington responded. The latter gentleman also proposed " The health of the Manager (Mr. W. H. Collier) and the members of the Bridgewater staff,"which was suitably ackn )wledged by Messrs. Ol- dfield, Meadowcroft,and Wiswall.—Mr. Collier sent a let- ter expressing his regret at being unable to be with them, aria spoke in high terms of the manner the staff general- ly had discharged their duties. Messrs. Harrison and Dudley,ef the Engineers'Department,Runcorn Yard,gave several humorous songs, and they were well supported by Captain Johnson, the pierinaster. Messrs. Clarke, Dowles, and Pickford also gave songs, which were much enjoyed. The meeting was brought ton close by a vote of thanks to the Chairman. Mr. Grounds acquitted himself very efficiently at the piano.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT WARRINGTON.

file aged people of Warrington had a good time of it on Thursday last week, when they were provided—the men with din- ner, :and the women with tea—at the a-I Hall. The sexagenarians and upwards ap- peared to enjoy themselves immensely, and they attacked the meat and other viands with the greatest of relish. In the evening, they were pro- vided with recreation in the shape of an excellent concert. It is astonishing to see so many people over 601 years of age in Warrington, and taking everything into account, it speaks well for tbe longevity of the TVarringtonians. If the" black spots" of the town were rem3ved, and the fever areas purified, the funds of the Treat Committee would, one would think, be strained to meet the demands made upon them.

lam glad to see that another of the death traps of Warrington is now a thing of the past. As eight persons have been drowned in what is generally spoken of as Bolton's pit, in Orford-lane, since 1885, it was high time that it should be filled up. The coroner was severe in his comments upon the latest death which was inquired into on Mon- day, and as a result, the fire engine was taken to the spot the very next day to pump out the water, preparatory to filling up the pit. It is to be hoped that this is the last of the " death-traps " of War- rington.

New Year's Day was,after all the rough weather,a very " seasonable " one—at least so said the skaters, who could be seen going in droves to indulge in their favourite pastime. The roads were also in excellent order for oycling, and this exercise was freely indulged in. IV arrington,in fact,bore a true holiday appearance during the day, and it is a long time since a winter holiday has been so much enjoyed.

It was generally expected that the gale of last Friday night and Saturday, coming so soon after the hurricane of the previous week, would do an immense amount of damage by finding the weak places left by the previous storm. Yet, fortunately, so far as Warrington is concerned, damage that has been done is of quite a minor character. Of course, there were plenty of loose slates and a few chimney pots lifted from their places,but these are regarded 'as the inevitable incidents of a storm. I am glad to see that not only did the tower of the Sacred Heart Church in Liverpool-road withstand the first gale, but that it successfully weathered the second, and looks none the worse for it.

In one place in Warrington, the old year went out, and the new year come in, with flames, and disaster. I allude to the premises of Messrs. S. E. and R. Johnson which were burnt down on that usually joyous occasion. It is a superstition that what is done on the New Year, will be done all the year round, but it is devoutly to be hoped that the fire engine will not be again as urgently required during the year as it was on New Year's morning. it was truly not a very happy omen for the firemen to be watching the New Year in with the hose pipes of the fire engine in their hands. The fire in ques- tion was a very large one, and it is extremely for- tunate that a gale similar to the previous Friday night was not blowing, or the result would have been apalling, considering the crowded state of property in the district around. As it was the dam- age was considerable, and there is much sympathy expressed with the workmen who are thrown tem- porarily out of work in consequence, and who in many cases have lost valuable:collections of tools.

--- Watchnight services are very popular, and in al the various churches and chapels of Warrington there were large congregations present at the ghostly hour of midnight on Monday last week. The holding of watchnight services is of comparatively recent date, but the idea has" caught on" well,and they are now established services which attract an increasing number of people each year. ;

The parish council meeting at Little Sankey passed off very quietly. The election of chairman was perfectly unanimous, and Mr. R. B. Matthews is now the head man in Little Sankey. The ever- lasting question of the borough extension was brought forward, as it has been at all the authorities near Warrington, and although nothing definite was done at the meeting, it is pretty evident that opposition will be made to the proposals of the Corporation. It is quite clear that the Corporation will have to fight for the extension. It is really wonderful what reluctance is shown by these "outsiders" to be included within the borders of the "good old town."

-- I notice that the Health .Committee has instructed the Medical Officer of Health and the Town Clerk to report on the subject of a public abattoir. This is a subject of the utmost importance. If a cattle market be established at the old Militia Barracks, as is now proposed. the vacant land adjoining the Barracks would, I should think, from an admirable site for an abattoir and the two being so closely situated to each other and of so easy access by road, rail or water, and with fields for pasture so near at I hand, would offer facilities for development of trade, local and general, that would be almost unrivalled in the United Kingdom.

The only semblance of opposition to such a scheme might be the quality of the neighbourhoool, but surely this is no sufficient reason to prevent the carrying out of such an excellent scheme. Sooner or later an abattoir will have to be built and the present slaughter-houses closed, as the Local Government Board are getting more and more stringent on the matter every year.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

Causcrt HISTORY LECTURES.—The Rev. G. W. Guest delivered another of his "Church History " lectures in the Newfield Institute, on M mday night. The lecture, which was illustrated with lantern slides, was on " The Growth of Papal Despotism in Britain from A.D. 1090 to A.D. 1265." The lantern was manipulated by Messrs. G. H. and H. Bayley. SEATING.—Owing to the severe frost of the past week this favourite winter pastime has been indulged in to the full, the dam and ponds in the neighbourhood being covered daily with skaters of every station in life. Several skaters have been immersed through the breaking of the ice, but up to the time of writing there has been no drowning fatality. THE NEWFIELD INSTITITTE.—A most successful con- cert took place at the above place on Saturday evening. In the absence of the Vicar, the Rev. J. T. Collins pre- sided. The first item on the programme was a song by Miss Grundy which was well received, as were also the songs of Miss Cookson, Miss Houston, the Misses Tod. hunter and Messrs. Gregson, Houston, Cartledge and Todhunter, the former receiving an encore. The last Item on the programme was a comic song by Mr. R. Dixon, which met with a meritorious encore, the audi- ence not being content until he had contributed a banjo

Selo. URBAN DISTRICT COIINCIL.—The first ordinary meet- ing of this Council was held on Tuesday evening in the Boardroom. Mr. Gregson presided, and there were also present—Dr. Williamson, Messrs. Gould, Brown, Mac- Intyre, Smith, Dewhurst. E. Holt, Appleton, Wel- ford, Mullard (clerk), Ridgway (law clerk), Dr. Fox (medical officer), and Mr. Mort (surveyor).— Dr. Fox submitted his annual report, which was passed, and on the motion of Dr. Williamson, seconded by Mr. Smith, fifty copies were ordered to be printed. A vote of thanks was also passed to the doctor for his report.— Sir. Brown moved that the question of an isolation hospital be submitted to the Sanitary Committee, and that they report to the next meeting of the Board.—Mr. Smith seconded the resolution, and it was carried.—The Gas Manager submitted his report, from which it ap- peared the illuminating power of the gas was 18 1-75 candles.—Mr. Smith moved "That provision be made for the office to be open daily."—lt was decided that it be considered in committee with other questions, and that the meeting be held on Monday night. ACTION AGAINST A SHOWMAN.—At the Manchester County Court, on Tuesday, before his Honour Judge Parry, an action was brought by a young man named Henry Johnson to recover £32 17s. 6d. for 51 weeks' ser- vice as assistant to Nr. James Shepherd, a Lymm show- man.—Mr. Wharton appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Langdon for the defendant.—Mr. Wharton said the plaintiff had been engaged as the showman's assistaat, at a salary of 15s. per week with board and lodgings. 'The defendant had paid the plaintiff a total of £5 7s. 6d. and the plaintiff had given him credit for it. The de- fendant told plaintiff that he wanted some person to go round with his caravan, and, though the salary the plaintiff at first asked was 21 a week, he ultimately ac- cepted the 15s. The plaintiff allowed defendant's wages to run on until he sold his show, and then, when asked for the wages due, the defendant told him that he had no hold on him, and refused to pay him. Subsequently, however, the defendant wrote to the plaintiff and said be would give him a£s note.—The plaintiff then gave evidence in support of Mr. Wharton's statement. Re- plying to questions, he said the show they travelled with contained a cow with a wooden leg and other curiosities and monstrosities.—Mr. Langdon, after addressing the Court, called the defendant, who said that no arrange- ment was made with the plaintiff. The plaintiff wanted to go with the show, and he (the defendant) took him On. The first week he gave him 55., the second week about 10s. and so on. The plaintiff said he wanted to get away from Manchester. Wages were never men- tioned. The plaintiff had the handling of all the aioney and helped himself.—His Honour gave judgment for the amount claimed with costs.

div.head: WARRINGTON DEBATING SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON DEBATING SOCIETY.

THE POLICY OF THE I.L.P. A debate took place at the monthly meeting of the Warrington Debating Society, which was held at the 'Masonic Rooms, Held-street, on Wednesday, upon the policy of the Independent Labour Party. The chair was occupied by Mr. Nield. Mr. Gee, the president of the local branch of the 1.L.P., in opening the subject, explained that the policy of the I.L.P. was socialistic. The first question v hich presented itself, he took it, was, what was socialism ? He would endeavour to give a definition which would be appreciable to every day lie. Socialism was an en- sieavour to substitute for the present inequitable struggle for existence, an organised co-operation for that existence. Ha contended that socialism was based upon the principles of sound political economy, and that the -evils which it opposed, were indisputable. Look at society to-day and compare these countries where the capitalistic system was properly devel- oped with those where the development had not been so advanced, and they would find far move poverty in the former countries. The socialists were opposed to the capitalists absorbing all the profits, which ought to go to the workers who made those profits. Capitalism!was a factor which had not always existed, and in the rude elements of scciety there was no capitalism. Socialism said that when there was depression, poverty,and de2re- dation, there must be a certain cause, and that cause was owing to the property classes who never did any- thing, taking the profits which shonld go to the workingmen who made that profit. They were astounded that at the last decade of the nineteenth century the workers of the country should be treated even worse than the worst savagr% The rapid develop- ment of machinery was the source of universal poverty and misery. He now alluded to a subject which he would rather have not mentioned, but it must be faced, and that was tha to-day. many of the crimes which were perpetuated were done under the name of religion. As a matter of fact, nine tenths of those who went to church .or chapels were workers, capitalists, or landlords, who were therefor the purpose of maintaining credit, and it appeared to him that the workers went there to keep their jobs at work, or to get the loaves and fishes. The socialists considered the state was the trustee for the people, and that the state should use the land, etc., for the benefit of the people. To show that the condition of the people wns relatively worse than it was 50 years ago, Mr. Gee gave some statistics which showed that the burdens were relatively lighter upon the rich than upon the poor, than they were at that time. People who did ..not. do work ought not to share in the profits, and he 'believed that an invention was only putting together What had been prepared by thousands of men previously. Mr. Gee then proceeded to denounce thrift. He said that this was the curse of mankind, and that the rich rn en were making their fcrtnnes upon the thrift of work- ingmen. He wished the workingmen of the country to throw off the curse of thrift. Mr. J. Horton said that he believed that it was for the benefit of humanity that the workers should get their honest share of the pr,fits for the work they do. He was a socialist to a certain extent. But they should not confine themselves to. the profession of principle; it was necessary to bring principle. to. practice. He contended that many co-operative societies had been the cause of distress to those who had put their faith in them. Let them take for example, Mr. Jabez Balfour. He (Mr. Horton) agreed with many of the statements made by Mr. Gee, hut he believed that they should move cau- tiously. He asked who were the cause of much of the low prices which necessitated the low wages paid to workingmen. Why members of the I.L.P. themselves, who were ever ready to buy at the hheapest shop. If the leaders of the party would en- deavour to counteract this thing they would do a good thing for the country. There were other causes for poverty in this country, and one great factor was drink. If drinking were put down, there would be far less cause to complain. The debate was continued by Messrs. Brouchemite, J. Gandy, J. Ainsworth, E. J. Hall, and Ball. The debate was then adjourned.

Mr. Gladaone, in ceivin nfl Monday An" address from a society of Irish americans, said he thought every Irish Nationalist should understand tga discord neces- sarily meant postnonemen,. of Irish claims. Eke earnestly hoped that sortie means would be found by which the different sections of the Irish party might be beadily brought together.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS

The first meeting of the above Board since the recent elections, was held on Wednesday morning, at the Work house. The members present were Mrs. Clay, the Revs- J. H. Riddette. Father Moore, and G. F. Roberts,Messrs. A. J. Jolley, S. Davies, T. Malkin,W. Hickman, A. Lang. G. Ratcliffe, W. Cross, J. Dignum, J. Houghton, J. Bil- linge, G. Thompson, J. W. Knowles,J. Clarke, A. Jolley, G. Pilling, T. Mather, E. L. Bent, T. Halton, H. Elibbert, W. Houghton, J. Johnson, Dr. Patterson, J. Ball, and J. Warburton. J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (deputy clerk), C. H. Ward (master), and H. M. Mines (superin- tendent). Upon vlrs. Clay entering into the room, she was in- troduced by Mr. Dignum, and the other members of the Board received her very cordially.
CHAIRMAN PRO. TEM.
On the motion of Mr. A. Jolley, seconded by Mr. J. Houghton, the Clerk was elected chairman pro. tem.
'EXPENSES OF THE ELECTIONS.

The CLERK then read a statement with regard to the expenses of the recent elections. The total cost of the uncontested elections amounted to £l2 133. 3d. The ex• penses for the township of Warrington which had a population of 57.000, a rateable value of £176,000, an electorate of 8,688, of which 6,366 were in the contested wards amounted to £9B 93. 6d., of which printing cost IEIS 193. In Haydock there were contests in all three wards, and the expenses amounted to £23 183. 31 The elections in Newton cost £2B 153. Bd.. and the total ex- pense to the union was £2ll 23. sd. The cost to the ratepayers in Warrington would be is. Bd. in the £,and in; Haydock fd. in the L. He said he was sure that this amount would compare favourably with many re- turns of elections throughout the country.

ion of the Board.—Mr„ BILLINGE thought there onght to be an unanimous vote in favour of the committee, tie hoped that in courtesy to the lady guard ;II ,lected,thev would form one, as it would be very uses . —Mrs. CLAY supported the proposal, and said that she knew several ladies who would be very willing to take up the duties which were required upon such a committee.—The CHAIRMAN said that they were now discussing the broad principle of forming, a ladies committee, and theylicould arrange details afterwards. He thought a trial should be given to the proposed committee.—The proposal to form a ladies' committee was carried by 14 votos to

nine. The Rev. J. H. RIDDETTE moved that the chairman, vice-chairmen, Mrs. Clay and Mr. Hickman be ap- pointed a sub-committee to decide upon ladies suitable for the Visiting Committee.—Mr. A. J. JOLLEY se- conded, Mr. BILLINGE supported, and the motion was carried. ----------

HOUSE COMMITTEE. The House Committee minutes were moved, seconded, and carried.—The CLERK said he had, on behalf of the children,to thank the following ladies and gentlemen for donations :—The Mayor and Mayoress, Lady GrePnall, Messrs. T. Lyons, John Crosfield, George Comber, &c. TRANSFER OF CHESHIRE PARISHES. The CLERK said that one of the difficulties they were troubled with was the time for the separation of the Cheshire parishes from this Union. He thought it would have been easier if the parishes had gone on un- til the end of March, because all the accounts of each half-year were made up at that time, and all balances brought forward. The tenor of a letter he had received from Mr. Ashton (Clerk to the Runcorn Board of Guar- dians), on 28th of lasi; month,was that he was going up to London the following day,and would call at the Local Government Board offices upon the question. Mr. Sutton had not since heard about the matter.

div.head: ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.
div.p: ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.

The CLERK then asked for nominations for the chair- manship of the Board until April Is.—The Rev. G. F. Roberts said that he welcomed Mrs. Clay to the Board, and thought that they would benefit very much from her presence. With regard to the chairmanship of the Board, be had great pleamire in proposing the election to the chair of Mr. William Houghton. That gentleman had presided over the deliberations of the old Board with very great credit to himself and also, he felt sure with the greatest possible satisfaction to every member of the old Board. It was said by Abraham Linooln that it was not wise to change horses while crossing the stream. Their position was changed from the old con- stitution to a new one, and he thought that the mem- bers should have the benefit of the old chairman's exper- ience for a short time at any rate. He felt sure he need not recommend Mr. Houghton to the old members of the Board, and he only wished to express the hope that the new members, until they became more acquainted with the work would to some extent utilise the experi- ence of the old members. He had therefore the greatest pleasure in proposing that Mr. William Houghton be the first chairman of the new Warrington Board of Guardians. —Mr. S. DAVIES had great pleasure in seconding the proposition. Mr. Houghton,he said, had won the utmost comfidence and respect of the members of the old Board, and he thought that in commencing their duties afeesh, it would be a great mistake if they did not place at the head of their affairs, a gentleman of large experience.— Mr. Diosium supported the motion. He said that Mr. Houghton was a very hardworking member of the Board, and was a very remarkably economical admint- trar of the poor law, and would not do anything to in- crease the rates of the parishioners.—Mr. THOMPSON, as a new member, also supported the motion, which was then put to the meeting and carried unanimously.—Mr. W. Houcurrox, in taking the chair, expressed his obi- • gation to the Board for again electing him. Fle said that he was afraid that from what had been said about him, • that some of the new members would be expecting too , much from him, but he would promise them to do his best, and he asked for the indulgence of th 9 Board during the time of his chairmanship. ELECTION OF VICE CHAIRMEN. _ _ _

The CHAIRM-A-N-Mo-ved, Mr. HIBBERT seconded, and I Mr. DIGNUM supported the election of Mr. S. Davies as senior vice chairman, and the motion was carried unani- mously.—Mr. DAVIES briefly replied.—Mr. A. J. Jotter thought that the Board should still have a junior vice chairman as before and he moved that Mr. G. Pilling occupy that post, and be the chairman of the Relief Committee.—Mr. J. HOUGHTON seconded, and the motion was carried.

DAY AND TIME OF MEETING. It was decided unanimously that it was unnecessary to change the day or time of the meeting of the Board Um the present,and aceprdingly the Board will con 111.10 to meet at 10.30 a.m. en every alternate Wednesday.

div.head: LONDON ANARCHISTS AND THE
div.p: LONDON ANARCHISTS AND THE
FRENCH SPY.

EXTRAORDINARY AFFAIR. The "Central News "says :—An extraordinary affair, which little more than a week ago put the entire Anarchist community in London into an uproar, has just been successfully investigated by " Central News" reporters. The facts are as follows :—About the end of August last year a young Frenchman arrived in the Anarchist quarter in London, apparently in a destitute condition. His sad case was brought to the notice of several French Anarchists, who took pity upon him, fed and clothed him, and found him some employment. The young man, who was known as Eugene, gained the con- fidence of the French Anarchists, and was admitted to their meetings. Towards the end of November, how- ever, it became evident to the Anarchists that their intentions and doings had become more than usually open to the knowledge of the secret police department in Paris, and suspicion began to fall upon the new com- rade. Through the miscarraee of an important docu- ment from Commissary Andr6 of the Third Brigade of Paris Police, suspicion was converted into certainty. A special meeting of the London foreign Anarchists was convened, to which Eugene was invited, and which he unsuspectingly attended. As soon as Eugene entered the room, he was seized and bound, kicked, cuffed, and spat upon. Itevolvers were held at his head and knives to his breast, and, thus coerced, he made a full confession of his relations with the French police. He proved to be a well-known agent named Cotin, alais Cuvilier, alias Cottance. Having made his confession, Cotin was thoroughly searched, and in a secret pocket was found an important letter, dated December 20th, from the Prefecture of Police, and marked "Urgent," in which Cotin, addressed as Cottance, was instructed to find out without delay everything that was then going on at Dieppe in connection with the movements of a certain lady, what business was about to bring her to London, who paid her travelling expenses, Izc. Other documents, said to be of considerable importance, were also found on Cotin. It was at first proposed te kill the spy, but more moderate counsels ultimately prevailed, and he .was simply kicked into the street, and ordered to leave London on pain of death. He immediately returned to Paris, and for his own safety has been placed in the Army, as the Anarchists have a portrait of Cotin, and are taking steps to circulate it in France.

div.head: SCANDALOUS STORY REFUTED.
div.p: A SCANDALOUS STORY REFUTED.

The "Daily Chronicle" reviewing the diplomatic reminiscences just published by the Baron de Malortie has the following remarks We cannot cite all the other, often very indiscreet, contents of the book, but there is one chapter which some of our contemporaries have signalised by quota- tion, and which is demonstrably incorrect. The veil throws over the characters is so thin that we do not hesitate to use the real names. The story, then, is that the present Duchess of Devonshire, when the young Duehess of Manchester, purchased by a kiss from the fourteenth Earl of Derby the written promise of the Mistress-ship of the Robes when he returned to power. The very first lines of the narrative show its apochry- phal character. "A long time ago, in the twenty-fifth year of the glorious reign of her most Gracious Majesty the Queen-Empress of the Waves "—so the opening runs. Now the twenty-fifth year was 1862. A party "was celebrating, at the spleadid seat of Lord X. (that is Lord Derby) the otium cunt dignit ate which an adverse Parliamentary vote had granted to a popular Prime Minister." But Lord Derby had been dismissed from ofEce in 1859 1 And there was no change of Government till 1865, when Lord Russell for a few months succeeded Lord Palmers- ton, not giving way Lord Derby until 1886. We are askiid to believe that Baron de Malortie, not even a naturalised Englishman at the time, was able to get a copy of &letter written by the Earl to the Duchess pro- mising her the revision of the highest post in the House- hold for a kiss publicly given ! The stately and fiery Earl is represented,when he did come back to power and was confronted with his written promise,as having been sure he could not obtain the Queen-Empress's consent to the nomination. There was no Queen-Empress until 1878-7 1 Lord X. (that is Lord Derby), was called to the Castle," presumably Wind;or Cate, and entrusted with the formation of a new Ministry." Very good. He, went to " Strutting-st. in order to pacify his impatient .creditor," the Duchess. She gave him " two hours to drive from " Strutting-street to the Castle," and " re- !turn with the coveted nomination," what time his new I Cabinet was waiting for its first meeting. When she got it she received it " with a fiendish smile." Well, cer- tainly if Lord Derby drove from London to Windsor r and back in two hours he could do any- thing. But of course the whole story is senilely silly, and arises from the fact that the nomina- tion of Her Grano of Manchester was a surprise to society. But it is intolerable that such incoherent rub- bish should he foisted upon readers during the lifetime, at any rate of the lady concerned. If this is Baron de Malortie's reading of the saying "Noblesse oblige," we could wish he had rem lined in fl mover instead of hon- ouring this country by being naturalised. And a de- monstrated falsehood of this sort throws grave doubts upon the rest of the book where we are not so easily able to test its very cenfident statements.

THE DANGER OF I SLIPPERY PAVEMENT. On Sunday night, Mrs. Sullivan, 12, Naylor-street, was walking along Butterrnarket-street, when she slipped on the footpath owing to the slippery nature of the ground, and sustained a broken leg. She was admitted to the Infirmary, where she will probably remain for a few weeks. • DEATH OF Mn. JOHN CROSS. On Saturday afternoon, at the age of 65 yeats, Mr. John Cross, who had carried on the business of a butcher in Warrington for about 40 years passed away at his residence, Corporation-St. The deceased had been in failing health for several months, although he attended to business as usual, until a week previous to his death, when his con- dition became so serious that he was relintantly compelled to retire to his bedroom. Ile had long suffered from bronchitis, and it was from this dis- ease that he died. Mr. Cross's life was not an eventful one, the greater part of his energies hav- ing been thrown into his business, but he was nevertheless well--known and greatly respected, and the news of his death, both in the town and coun- try, will be read with general regret. He leaves a family of seven children to mourn his loss, Mrs. Cross having died three years ago. The funeral took place at the Cemetery on Tuesday afternoon in the , presence of a large number of relatives and friends. The corttige left Corporation-St. about half-past two o'clock, several shopkeepers in the neighbourhood displaying their respect to the deceased by either lowering their blinds or placing shutters against their windows. Followil.4 the hearse were six carriages, the chief mourners being :—Messrs. Ben- jamin, John, and Samuel Cross (sons), Mr. John Myles (son-in-law), Broadheath ; Messrs. J. W. and Thomas Southern, ;•alford ; Mr. Clare, Widnes; NIT. Peter Lawless, Councillor Shillcock, Mr. Smith, and Mr. Tapley (nephews). The body was enclosed in a coffin composed of English oak, heavily mounted with brass, and bearing the following inscription: —"John Cross, died January sth, 1894, aged 65 years." After the short service in the cemetery chapel, the coffin, which was almost covered with floral tributes, was borne to the grave on the shoul- ders of Messrs. John Wainwright,Clough,H. Mather, Frank Connolly, Peacock, and Everall. The burial service was conducted by the Rev. It. H. M. Hutt, one of the curates of the Parish Church.

' At Blackburn on Wednesday Joseph Noble, secretary of tne Rishton Co-operative Society. and John Noble, clerk, father and son, were committed for trial OR a charge of forging a cheque on the Society. The father pleaded guilty, and exonerated his son. The father is , also charged with orthezeing £l2O. It was stated that the total defalcations amounted to £1,700.

DEAN TRUST CHARITY EXHIBITION. Last week we gave the result of the examination held in connection with the Dean Charity Trust. On Wednes- day the committee met to consider the examiner's re- port, and seeing that one of the competitors, Edwin Longworth, of Newton School, was only two marks be- hind the third successful competitor, the committee decided to award him an exhibition. Sr. PFTER'S DAY SCHOOLS, NEWTON. The annual examination of the scholars attending the above schools should have been held during December, but an intimation has been received from the Depart- ment, to the effect that this year the school will be exempt. The school must be in a high state of efficiency, when the Department do not consider it necessary to examine the children. NEWTON DIVISION BOWLING ASSOCIATION. Owing to the chailenge cup which was given by the Hon. T. W. Legh, M.P. to be played for by the bowling clubs in the Newton Division, having been won out- right by the North Ashton club, the committee found themselves at the end of last season, in the position of being without an object for competition. They however approached the Hon. T. W. Legli on the subject, and on the matter being represented to him, he very kindly ,offered another challenge cup to be competed for by the dubs. _

THE WEATHER. During the week, the roads and bye-ways in Earle-- town and Newton have been frost-bound, making it difficult for pedestrians to get about with safety. Most of the shallow pools of water have been frozen and youngsters have enjoyed themselves :skating There have been one or two accidents on the deeper ponds, owing to the treacherous nature of the ice. At the Common pit on Saturday, a man was immersed up to the neck, and two lads had a narrow escape from drown- ing in a pond at War grave. The frost has not been sufficiently severe to cover the lake at Newton, although at one end it has been thinly scarfed with ice. EARLESTOWN TRADESMEN'S SOIREE.

The second annual soiree under the auspices of the Earlestown tradesmen, was held in the Town Hall, Earlestown, on Wednesdaysevening. There was a large number of people present, and dancing, which was commenced at nine o'clock, was kept up until about four o'clock on Thursday morning, to music supplied by Mr. Peplow's string band. At intervals songs were given by Miss Aaen, Messrs. S. Swann. G. Kidd, J. Williams, and W: Attfield, and Mr. J. Howard gave whistling solos. Mr. W. Thompson accompanied the various songs. The refreshment bar was under the charge of Mr. R. Lythgoe. GOOD TEMPLARY (EBENEZER LODGE). The Earlestown Ebenezer Lodge of Good Templars held its weekly session on Tuesday evening in the Co- operative Hall. Bro. A. Morris, C.T., presided, and there was a good attendance of members and visitors. Two candidates were admitted to membership, and Bro. J. Singleton read the digest of No. 1 Convention to be held at Hindley. Bro. W. J. Taylor gave report of New Year's tea party, and Bro. A. Morris tendered fraternal greetings from Latchford Lodge. Bro. J. Taylor did the same from Mission Lodge, Warrington. The programme for the evening was " short readings," the following taking part :—Bros. Brown J. Singleton, A. Morris, W. Morris, J. Taylor, W. Taylor, J. Jones, and Williamson. GOOD TEMPLARY. The usual weekly session ef the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars was held in the Co-operative Hall, on Monday evening. Bro. Joseph Anderton, P.C.T. presided, and there was a good attendance of members. Two candidates were initiated and several others proposed. The digest of business for No. 1 Con- vention to be held at Hindley on Saturday was read by Sister Warburton, L.D., and arrangements were made for representatives to attend. It was decided to pay a visit to the Hope of Vulcan Lodge, and a committee was appointed to make arrangements. Bro. C. Willis, sem, I tendered greetings from the femperance Mission and Wesley Lodge, Warrington, of which he gave a good account, and which he said were doing well. Several other items of business were transacted. The programme of the evening was " a night with the juniors," Bro. W. Wilson being responsible. A good programme of songs and recitations was given, and an interesting meet ing closed the usual way. FORMATION OF IL CYCLING CLUB AT EARLESTOWN. A meeting was held at the New Market Inn, Earles- town, on Thursday evening, for the purpose of forming a cycling club for E irlestown. Mr. T. Bowes presided, and there was a fair number present. After deciding to torm a club, bearing the title of the" Earlestown Social Cycling Club," with headquarters at the New Market Inn, the election of officers was proceeded with. Mr. I'. • Waring was elected hon. secretary, Mr. T. Robinson treasurer, committee, Dr. Patterson (chairman), T. Hamer (vice-chairman), T. Bowes, F. Gerrard, P. Brad- shaw, T. Robinson and Austin. Mr. P. Bradshaw was elected captain and Mr. T. Bowes vice-captain. A deputation was appointed td wait on a gentleman to solicit his acceptance . f the office of president. It was resolved that all honorary members be vice-presidents. A code of general rules was submitted and adopted, together with road rules. The subscription for ordinary members was fixed at 53. per annum. CHRISTIAN MEETING Room. On Tuesday evening, in connection with the Improve- ment Class, a very interesting lecture was given by Mr. J. H. Harrison (an undergraduate of University College, Liverpool) on" Ammonia." The chair was occupied by Mr. G. S. Kin, and there was a good atteada,nce. In explaining the origin of the word " Ammonia," Mr. Harrison said the Labs in the desert of Lybia first made Sal ammoniac—a compound of ammonia—by burning camel's dung near the Temple of Jupiter Ammon, and hence the name Ammonia. This substance was one of the few known to the ancients. The old alchymists when searching for the Philosopher's stone which was to turn all the basrr metals into gold, and the Elixir of life which was to indefinitely prolong life, were aware of its properties, and it is referred to by Pliny under the name of " Vehement Odour." Priestley first carefully experi- mented on ammonia, which he called "Alkaline alr." The lecturer showed that the gas was a compound con- sisting of one atom of nitrogen and three of hydrogen, and by the aid of experiments showed the properties of the gas. At the close a number, of facts 'were given about this substance and its compounds. It was stated that a man gives off in one way or another twenty-two to twenty-seven grammes of ammonium sulphate per 24 hours or 17 to Albs. per annum. If all the ammonium sulphate obtainarle trom London were procured, we should have 60,000 tons of ammonium sulphate p annum. In Paris the refuse which amounts to 2,200 tons per 24 hours is collected and treated with milk ot lime and is allowed to settle ' • the liquid is worked for ammonia and the mud is heated by steam, passed through a filtering process, then taken and pressed into ' cakes which are sold as manure. Coal varies in the oubittainLabalnecfarsohmireit accordingoal contains t2h; amountu n t mo per cent. of nitro,en Welsh .91 per cent., Newcastle amount of ammonianitrogen 1.32, and Scotch 1.44 It is calculated that 400,000,000 tons of coal are used annually in Great Britain ; but 90 per cent. is not used for the recovery of ammonia; if all were so used we should have from this source 26 million tons of ammonium sulphate annually. The uses were then referred to. During the lecture many experiments were performed. The audience were invited to ask questions, the lecturer ans wering them satisfactorily. A sad death, due to the effects of the inhalation of gas from vitriol chambers, occurred at St. Helens early on Wednesday morning, the victim being thigh M'Cabe, 27 years of age, of 21., Victoria-street, Gerard's-bridge. ThA deceased man was a chemical labourer, and was iainployed at the Globe Works of the United Alkali Com- pany. He and three other men were deputed to clean out one of the vitriol chambers on Tuesday, and in the course of the afternoon one of the men complained of illuoss and ceased operations for the day. M'Cabe con- tinued to work, hcwever, though he, too, complained of !pains in his he.Ad just before he " knocked off" work at five o'clock. On reaching his lodgings he told the land- lady that he had bees " gassed " and felt very unwell. , She at once gave him a cup of tea and a glass of water, the customary remedies in such cases, and M'Cabo went to bed. He, however, grew much writ and Dr. Fred Knowles was sent far. That gentleman found M'Cabe to be suffering from the effects of the inhalation of gas, and prescribed accordingly, but all Pfforrs to save tins man's life were unavailing, and he died shortly after midnight.

NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.

THE ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.—LIVELY- MEETING. The first meeting of the newly-elected Newton Urban District Council, was held on Monday, at the Earles- town Town Hall. The members present were Councillors J. W. Emmett, R. Stone, J. Smith, J. Simpson, C. B. F. Borron, C.C., P. MacMahon, J. Slee, W. Beattie, T. Ormand, G. Ratcliffe, F. T. Evans, W. Gilmour. W. Collingwood, W. Thompson, F. J. Wood, J. E. Worseley (law clerk), R.Brierley (clerk and surveyor).

ELECTION OF TEMPORARY CHAIRMAN.—TIIE FIRST DIVISION OF THE MEMBERS. As soon as the councillors had taken their seats, Mr. Smith moved that Mr. R. Brierley, their clerk, and the returning officer at the late election, take the chair pro tern.—Mr. G.Ratcliffe seconded.—Mr. Gilmour said that in all his experience of Councils, the chairman of the old Council took the chair until a new chairman was appointed, and Mr. Outland also contended that the , returning officer had not the power to take the chair.— Mr. Smith : That is not my experience.—Mr. Ormand then moved and Mr. Gilmour seconded that Mr. Emmett take the chair. Upon a vcte being taken, there voted for Mr. Emmett, Messrs. MacMahon, Evans, Ormand, and Gilmour, four ; for Mr. Brierley, Messrs. Wood, Stone, Simpson, Smith, Thompson, Slee, Coßingwood, and Beattie, eight. Mr. Brierley was accordingly elected.—Mr. Ratcliffe : Can Mr. Brierley give a cast- ing vote.—Mr. Ormand : No, he has no power.
ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.--LIVELY DEBATE.

Mr. Brierley then asked for nominations for the chair- manship of the Council. A considerable period elapsed before anyone arose, but at length, Mr. R. Stone rising said that he had been waiting for some member of the old Board to express his views with regard to the chair- manship of the Council,but as none of them had arisen, he did so. He proposed the name of Mr. C. B. P. Borren for the position. Mr. Borron was so well known to the ratepayers in the township, that it was net at all neces- sary to speak of his qualifications. He had always as- sisted in any movement which was conducive to the good of the inhabitants. Ile bad been for some time the manager of the schools in Newton and Earlestown, and in all the public offices which he had undertaken he had shown a willingness and desire to work for the benefit of the ratepayers. He was also their representative on the County Council, and he (Mr. Stone) thought it was to the advantage of the Council that they should have a member who was on the County Council as their chair- man,as there might be some matters which would have to be referred to the County Cuuncil.and on which,by hav- ing Mr. Borron present,time might be saved. Some years ago Mr. Borron had served the ratepayers as a Commis- sioner for a short time, and many ratepayers he had spoken to had regretted that Mr. Barron had not con- tinued a member of the Board. He was sure that no- thing would give more pleasure to the whole of the rate- payers in that district, than the election of Mr.Borron as chairman. Mr. J. Slee seconded the name of Mr. Borron. Mr. T. Ormand said that as a member of the old Boardjhe abstained from rising because ha thought some new member would have had the graciousness to have proposed the re-election of the old chairman, Mr. James Watson Emmett. He (the speaker) had been a member of the Newton Commissioners for four and a half years, and during the whole of that time, Mr. Emmett had acted in the:position of chairman with ability, and there was nothing which could be brought against him. He had gone before the ratepayers, and they had expressed themselves satisfied. Be had con- tested the largest and most difficult ward in the town and that ward had recorded its pleasure by returning him at the top of the poll. It would be a gracious act on the part of the Council to re-elect Mr. Emmett as first chairman of the district council. Personally ha had nothing to say against Mr. Borron, and another year he would have had great pleasure in supporting him as chairman, but be must ask them to receive as an amend- ment the nomination of Mr. Emmett as chairman of the Council. Mr. G. Ratcliffe seconded the amendment. He said that Mr. Emmett had served 27 years on the Commis- sioners, and he was connected with the largest railway company in England. He had served the late Board with great ability, and therefore he ought to have the honour of being first chairman of the new Council. Mr. Gilmour said that it was the wish of the majority of the ratepayers that Mr. Emmett should have been unanimously elected chairman of the Council. Mr. Barron had been a member of the late Commissioners. but he had been pitchforked in by the good pleasure of the Board, and the present occasion was the first time he had been elected by the ratepayers. He did not think they would be acting exactly honourably if they did not re-elect Mr. Emmett. Be thought Mr. Borron ought to be vice chairman, and he was not in favour of a man being chairman for along period, but it was an act of courtesy to re-elect Mr. Emmett. Mr. MacMahon also supported the nomination of Mr. Emmett, as lie had been a well-tried chairman, and had served the township well. There ought not to be a divided vote upon the subject, as Mr. Emmett had the confidence of the whole township. Mr. Smith said that he had been 'a member of the Commissioners for a short time, and could bear testi- mony to the courtesy which Mr. Emmett had always shown. At the same time he was sorry to say that he could not support hin, on the present occasion, as he be- lieved thatthe ratepayers desired a change. He thought Mr. Borron, was well qualified for the post. He must again state his belief that there was a very widespread feeling that there should be great changes on the Board. Mr. E. T. Evans supported the nomination of Mr. Emmett, as it was an act of courtesy to elect him. Mr. Simpson reminded the Council that Mr. Emmett had been chairman of the late Board for over four years. He believed that there ought to be radical changes on the Council. Mr. Borron had been instrumental in hav- ing the township divided into wards, and thus given Newton an opportuoity of being represented whilst the late Commissioners opposed it, and he wouid vote for him for that as well as for other reasons. Mr. Emmett said that Mr. Simpson was not correct in saying that the late Board was opposed to the division of the township into wards. They were desirous of waiting until the Parish Councils Bill had passed, and then they would have moved in the matter. He re- gretted to see that Mr. Smith had turned round upon him, for it was as an act of courtesy that he (Mr. Emmett) had asked Mr. Smith personally to fill the vacancy on the Board. It was, therefore, a surprise to him that Mr. Smith had turned the tables upon him. Mr. Smith: No, no. Mr. Gilmour: I know the reason why. Mr. Smith: It is very ungracious for any member to says he knows the reason why I acted in any capacity. Mr. Gilmour does not know. We are going to betroubled with this man. Mr. Emmett: You have no right to say that. I was taken aback, Mr. Smith, when you said you could not give me your support, seeing that I have been the means of bringing you to be a Commissioner. Mr. mit h : It was very much against your wish I wrote a letter declining the Offer first. Mr. Emmett: I am perfectly sure you never did write declining it, in any shape or form. Mr. Smith: I certainly did, and I could produce the , letter. Mr. Emmett: If you will produce your letter well and good. But lam quite certain that no letters to that effect ever passed between us. So far from writing declining the offer, it was quite the reverse. Mr. Smith : But I certainly did write. The names were then put to the meeting, and for Mr. Emmett, there voted Messrs. Ratcliffe, MacMahon, Gilmour, Ormand and Evans, five for Mr. Borron, Messrs. Wood, Stone, Simpson, Smith, Thompson, Slee, Collingworo and Beattie, eight. Mr. Borron was therefore elected chairman until April 15. Mr. Borrnn,on taking the chair, thanked the members for electing him. He felt the responsibilities of the situation, and would endeavour to act impartially. He was not in favour of the chairmanship being limited to any one individual, and thought that other members ought also to be elected to that honourable office. ELECTION OF VICE-CHAIRMAN. Mr. Wood prolonged, and Mr. Thompsoniseconded the election of Mr. Collingwood is vice-chairman of that Board. Mr. Gilmour proposed and Mr. Ratcliffe seconded the election of air. Ormand, Mr. Eataffe stating as his reasomthat Mr. Colling.wood was a very bad attender. Henn the names being put to the meeting, Messrs. Emmett, RAteliffe, NtlicMahon, Gilrnaur, Evans, and Beattie, voted for Mr. Ormand,and Messrs. Wood, Stone Smith, Simpson, Thompson, Slee, and the chairman, for Mr. Collingwnod. Mr. Cellingwood was therefore de- clared elected by seven votes to^six. Mr. Collingwnnd briefly replied. DAY AND TIME OF MEETING, Mr. Gilmour proposed, and Mr. Collingwood seconded that the Council meetings in future be at six o'clock in theirvening of the first Monday in the month. Mr. Smith moved as an amendment, and Mr. Wood seconded that the time remain as at present. Mr. Evans moved that the day be altered to Thursday e 6.30 p.m., hut as there was no seconder, the motion fell to the ground. Upon the amendment being put to the meeting, the following voted for it. Messrs. Smith. Stone, Wood, MacMahon, and SIPE., five for the motion, there voted, Messrs Emmett, Ratcliffe, Gilmour, Simpson,Thompson Collingwosd, Evans, Beattie, and Ormand, nine. The meetings will therefore in future be held at six o'clock on the first Monday in each month. A WIC o—THE FIRST LINANIMOUS VOTE. On the motion of Mr. Ormsnd, seconded by Mr. Smith, six was fixed as the number to form a quorum. This was the first unanimous vote of the Council. FINE FOR NOI4-ACCEPTANCE OF OFFICE. On the motion of Mr. Gilmore, seconded by Mr. Emmett, Was fixed as the fine for non-acceptaime or resignation of office. TITLE OF THE BOARD. Mr. Smith moved, and Mr. Stone seconded that the title of the Board be " The Urban District Council, for Newton-in-Makerfieid," and the Clerk be empowered to make a seal. div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN.

(BY AN OCCASIONAL CONTRIBUTOR). "They have been and gone, and done it," Such was the expression made use of several times when it became known that Mr. Emmett had not been elected chairman of the New Council. To a great many people this came as a surprise, but your humble servant is not included in this number. Oh no, I was in the know, and was pretty well aware of what was coming, but still as an act of courtesy or graciousness, or whatever you like to call it, I thought the Board would not be so ill-advised, as to scatter to the winds the long and tried services of an old Commissioner, in favour of a practically brand new man. But they have not taken my ad- vice,and as a consequence, Mr. Emmett has by force of circumstances been passed over. Some of those composing the Council fancy themselves wise acres but I cannot see any wisdom in the action they have taken. Perhaps I am dense; well, let it be 10.

Nevertheless I have an opinion, and being at large in a free country, am at liberty to give expression to it,just as much as the Councillors who have raised all the hubbub, of course I am not going to deny that some people will gloat over what they call the downfall of Earlestown, but it must not be supposed that these eight wise Councillors have acted exactly as their constituents would -,fish. In fact I doubt very much whether they have consulted anything but their own personal feelings in the matter. Mr. Stone said the election of Mr. Borron would meet with the approval of the majority of the ratepayers. This was very good as an opening, for Mr. Stone, but'which section of the ratepayers did he allude to? If to Newton, then his statement could hardly be correct, because Newton does not possess the majority, which is proved by the election returns. If he referred to Viaduct Ward or Town Hall ward, it still could not be correct, as the representatives of both these wards supported Mr. Emmett's nomi- nation. Mr. Smith trotted out quite a new and startling excuse—he said the ratepayers desired an entire change. That was sweeping assertion, and , Mr. Gilmour fitly described it as nonsense, which considerably roused Mr. Smith's ire.

It must not be imagined that I object to Mr Borron personally. He may be a very capable man and no doubt is, but the tactics pursued to secure his election, can hardly be said to be in consonance with the general wish of the ratepayers. Evidently the election of chairman was fought out on party lines, and as the Conservatives are in the majority, we may expect some startling developments ere long. At the outset they were apparently ashamed of their intended action, else why should they de- sire to come to an arrangement before going in the presence of the press. Mr. Emmett took the right course and refused to be a party to any hole and corner business.

This, however, from what I can hear was only a blind, on the part of the Tories, as I learn they met in solemn conclave on the preceding Saturday, and made all their arrangements, going to the Council meeting with a cut and dried programme. If this is how the town's business is to be dealt with, we must keep our hands to the plough, and be on the alert, and active for the next elections, and see if the scale cannot be a little more evenly balanced.

--- Even Mr. Ormand's long services were passed over, and by the casting vote of the chairman, he , lost the position of vice-chairman. Whatever the ratepayers wanted, the Tory party in the Council determined to have an entire change,and they have got it. Mr. Collingwood has been made chairman of the Highway Committee, and it will be interest- ing to notice whether he will be able to keep the roads in any better condition than they have been kept lately. Anyhow there are apparently stirring times in store, but I hope working-men will assert their right and attend the monthly meeting, when they .will see for themselves who are their champions.

HALF-HOUR TALKS IN THE LIBRARY. On Thursday evening another of the half-hour talks about books and their authors, was given, in Runcorn Free Library by Mr. J. J. Ogle, librarian and lecturer of the Bootle Free Library and Museum There was a good attendance. Councillor E. Imison, J.P., introduced the lecturer, and said those lectures had proved more interesting than the promoters anticipated. He could safely pro- mise that, if the interest was maintained, betore next season better arrangements would be made.- (Applause.) They had a man with them that night who was quite an expert in the management of public libraries. • He was not a man with a single Idea, but a many sided man. He took an interest in the works of art, and was also a capable and pro- minent botanist—Mr. Ogle prior to his lecture,said he had only been in Runcorn a few hours, but be had had the very great pleasure ot going through the Technical Institute. He hoped the wiePle Runcorn were going to rodui of it for the bene- fit of themselves and tir hildren. He (the speaker) had been a working-man. He worked. as an apprentice and for some time afterwards,betore he went into library work. He knew their wale and difficulties, but he believed education We' the one lever which would lift them up. (Applause) They were a happy people in Runcorn to have suc_li an institution. Mr. Ogle then proceeded with his half-hour lecture on " Cowper." IL did not P. Cowper amongst the great poets. He held the pos'-- don of one who was not above people of very moderate comprehension, and yet was so hialir to lead them on to something better. After briel'A‘r passing in review the early life of Cowper, to' referring to the causes leading to his madness, the lecturer said Cowper was more than 50 years of age when his first volume of poetrylo49., published. A number of his poems were then reau including the one entitled "The Task." Not onlY would Cowper be remembered as a poet but sea' letter writer. There was a beautful naturalness in his letters and they were considered by solre critics to be superior to his poetry. Referring rn the ballads of Cowper the lecturer said t_lit° although he could not be diassed with humorists. there was quite a fund of humour in his ballade; "John Gilpin "was mentioned as an instance, another ballad ballad entitled "Pairing time anticipated was read. Speaking of the odes written by CoisPeri the lecturer said that " The Loss of the 13,03.6 d George" was one of the finest funeral odes that he: been penned. After reading "Boadicea' spotlit_ ode by Cowper, the lecturer concluded by rece_in mending his hearers to read several books referring.. to Cowper and his works.—A hearty vote of than? was accorded the lecturer on the proposition of xr. William Handley, seconded by Mr. J. D. Jones.

div.head: PADGATE WESLEYAN TEA PARTY.
div.p: PADGATE WESLEYAN TEA PARTY.

The annual tea party and entertainment in connection with the Padgate Wesleyan Sunday School was held in the schoolroom on Tuesday evening. The tea was well attended, and admirably served. At the subsequent entertainment the room was crowded, Mr. W. Bennett

presiding. Mr. F. WRITE, the secretary of the Sunday school, read his report of the school work during the past year, which was as follows:—" The population of Padgate has been increasing very much of late years, and we are pleased to state that a steady increase has been main- tained in the number of our scholars. We have now 102 girls and 92 boys, making a total of 194 attending the school, an increase of 22 during the year. The attend- ance has been good, the average being 83 in the,morning and 157 in the afternoon. The teachers and officers number 25, of whom 11 are male and 14 female, and I am pleased to say we are now very well equipped with both male and female teachers. The officers appointed for the ensuing year are—Superintendents, Messrs. F. Wright and H. Ward ; treasurer, Mr. Frank Harris ; secretary, Mr. F. White ; club secretary and librarian, Mr. E. Andrews. As to the finances, the receipts for the year have been £5l 12s. 10d., and the expenses £34 19s 81., which leaves a balance in hand of £l6 13s. 2d. Out of this the treasurer has placed the sum of £lO to- wards the fund for the enlargement of the schools, thus leaving a workable balance of £6 13s. 2d. Whilst very cordially thanking the friends for their very generous support of the school,the contemplated enlargement will be a heavy strain on the funds, and the teachers and offi-ers ask and hopefully rely on an increased support in the coming year. A new branch of work has just been successfully started in connection with the school. I refer to the Young People's Recreative Society. Mr. H. E. Roscollar has been appointed president, Mr. J. C. Harrington,vice- president, Mr. Ernest Andrews secretary, and a strong committee has been formed. The Band of Hope has been re-organized, and under the leadership of Quarter- master-Sergeant Mantle is doing a good work. The sum of £67 has been paid into the Clothing Club during the year by 25 scholars, as against £4l 183. for 1893, which shows an increase in the deposits this year of £25 2s. The free library, which consists of 300 books of useful literature, is well patronized. Altogether our school is in a very satisfactory and, I think we may say, prosper- ous condition." The Chairman congratulated the officers upon the lexcellent report of the Secretary, and said they were again face to face with the fact that they were short of room. It was a very pleasing fact,, and the trustees would have to take into consideration what extension should he made, before very long. The Rev. J. Gunnell, in the course of an interesting address, said it was a pleasure to him to know that they were making steady progress in their Sunday school. The secretary's report was most encouraging. The average attendance at the school on an afternoon was very high. It was only a very short time since the chapel had been enlarged, when a most needful addition was made, and now they foand themselves straitened for Sunday school purposes. He knew when they took such a thing as the enlargement of their Sunday school into their heads and hearts they would very soon do it. The musical and vocal part of the entertainment had been excellently arranged by Miss M. Bennett and Miss H. Howard, and passed of very successfully. r RETIREMENT OF SERGEANT PLAYER, OF RUNCORN. Drill-Instructor Sergeant Player, of Runcorn, will next week retire on a pension, after a long service of 36 years. For 18i years Sergeant Play or was with the Cheshire Regiment, and during that time visited many quarters of the globe, but always had the fortune to escape actual warfare. Nearly 18 ears ago be was drafted to Runcorn to fill the position of instructor to the local companies of the 2nd Cheshire Rifle Volunteers, and he has acted in that capacity until the present time, proving him- self a smart soldier and a capable drill master. tie I is to be succeeded by Sergeant-Instructor Callaghan of Lymm, who is being transferred from the 3rd Cheshire Volunteers. Sergeant Callaghan has put in almost 30 years' service in the Cheshire Regiment and the Cheshire Volunteers.
